Deep learning models' effectiveness in semantic segmentation and other tasks relies on first learning general visual patterns with a suitable pre-training strategy. To support this claim, we introduce a novel approach called NetPlop, a large-scale, efficient, and highly reproducible framework for pre-training, allowing for the simultaneous training of multiple network architectures on the same dataset. We then compare the effectiveness of different pre-training tasks, including a novel study on using unsupervised depth estimation to enhance semantic segmentation. For this, we've made publicly available the full training pipeline and validation metrics, including rare ground truths, to facilitate the proper evaluation of pre-training techniques. Our key finding shows that unsupervised depth estimation pre-training can yield around 4% better performance than a widely accepted benchmark on the Cityscapes dataset. Notably, we've observed considerable improvements on smaller datasets as well. These gains suggest that depth estimation can serve as a more effective pre-training task for semantic segmentation than more conventional approaches, and we're confident that NetPlop will facilitate the exploration of a wide range of pre-training tasks and methods in the future. Our team has achieved this simplification by transforming the underlying problem into a determinant calculation. Specifically, we have shown that the well-known rank correlation statistic can be expressed as a product of two determinants. A predator-prey model based on Holling-Tanner's optimal environmental windows, with an added nonlinear response for Allee effects on prey population, has been introduced and analyzed. This system, characterized by a nonlinear Allee-type curve for prey population dynamics, reveals the existence of complex dynamics, including both generalized bistability and partial Allee effects. Furthermore, bistability is shown to arise from three coexisting solutions - a predator-only equilibrium, a prey-only equilibrium, and a predator-prey cycle. Additionally, our findings include a half-center type island, a generalized saddle-neighbor to a half-center, and a generalized saddle-neighbor to a predator-prey cycle. This analysis also discusses how parameters can be adjusted to replicate diverse patterns observed in real-world populations, including generalized Hopf bifurcations, Hopf bifurcations with stability loss, non-generalized Hopf bifurcations, and period-doubling bifurcations. This work contributes to our understanding of how environmental pressures affect population dynamics in predator-prey systems. We have also demonstrated numerically how such pressures influence the long-term behavior of these systems, including transitions from periodic to constant states and the creation of oscillatory patterns. This study has also shown numerically that when prey population responds non-linearly to increases in their own density, complex dynamics arise, including a predator-prey cycle coexisting with a predator-only equilibrium, a half-center type island, a generalized saddle-neighbor to a predator-prey cycle, a generalized Hopf bifurcation, a period-one orbit, a period-two orbit, and a period-five orbit. These findings highlight the significance of considering nonlinear responses of ecological populations in understanding ecological mechanisms. Finally, we have shown numerically that when both predator and prey populations respond non-linearly to increases in their respective densities, complex dynamics arise, including a predator-prey cycle coexisting with a half-center type island, a generalized saddle-neighbor to a predator-prey cycle, a generalized Hopf bifurcation, a period-one orbit, a period-two orbit, and a period-five orbit. This work provides a framework for understanding how environmental pressures influence the long-term behavior of ecological systems. It also provides a method for incorporating nonlinear responses of ecological populations in modeling ecological mechanisms. We analyze families of time-regular perturbations of Lindblad operators acting on a finite number of fermionic modes, where each mode has a finite dimension. By leveraging high-rate expansions in the perturbation strength, we derive explicit formulas for the long-term dynamics, including the steady state and spectral flow through the subspace of normalized fermionic states. Our findings reveal that the long-term behavior of the reduced density matrix tracks the behavior of a time-regular perturbation of a scalar Schrödinger operator of the form $V(u)\partial_t\varphi=\big((H_0+u(t))\varphi\big)$. Furthermore, the conditions that allow for a zero steady state or isolated isolated eigenvalues of the reduced density matrix correspond to those of a time-regular family of elliptic operators. Our work is inspired by recent advancements in mathematical physics, specifically non-linear quantum optimal control and related investigations involving fermionic systems. It has significant implications for the analysis of fermionic QED and the Bogoliubov ladder in quantum information theory. Moreover, the methods employed build upon previous research on high-rate expansions for scalar regularizations of PDEs and their application to PDE-based control problems, extending to operator-valued functions and reduced density matrices. Additionally, we demonstrate the convergence of approximate solutions to the exact one in a data-dependent manner, facilitated by the use of a minimum principle for $V(u)$. Our findings complement existing research, including a recent publication that analyzed time-irregular perturbations of Lindblad operators. Unlike that work, the current research involves time-regular perturbations, which have greater practical applications, but are less general in terms of the admissible perturbations. However, in many instances of interest, including the main examples presented in this study, the set of time-regularized initial data aligns with the set of time-irregular initial data. Finally, this work establishes relationships between multiple formulations of the long-term dynamics, including the standard Lindblad equation, its associated Markov semigroup, and its steady state. Moreover, it shows that the Markov semigroup acting on the subspace of normalized fermionic states is strongly convergent in a data-dependent manner to a semigroup generated by a time-regularized scalar Schrödinger operator. These findings are instrumental in the analysis of fermionic systems, where multiple time scales often emerge due to different evolution speeds, leading to separate Markovian and non-Markovian components. Large-scale classification and categorization tasks are typically handled by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). However, these models can be compromised if their core structure is imitated with a smaller network, making them easier to manipulate and evade, particularly in security-related image analysis and recognition systems. This study investigates various techniques for transferring DNNs, emphasizing their impact on performance and accuracy. We assessed these transfers using accuracy rates, a measure known as Mean Average Precision (mAP), and the ability to classify images. Our analysis involves migrating datasets between three main areas of computer vision: object detection, self-driving car navigation, and self-driving truck visualization. Our goal is to understand which DNN structure and whether using which training materials result in the most accurate image identification and classification. In this study, we also explored techniques to mitigate the accuracy loss common in DNN domain migration by incorporating transfer learning. Our findings can inform designers on how to successfully transition DNNs, manage accuracy loss, and improve image analysis systems even when the model's core structure is changed without affecting its core functionalities. Moreover, our research demonstrates how to adapt these transitions in DNNs on a small-scale model to a large-scale distribution of the same model without affecting the outcome. DNNs on a large-scale model can also be migrated without affecting the performance even when the core structure is changed. However, this idea expands upon the work of Nassim Nicholas Taleb in "The Bed of Procrustes" by examining the variety of ways to represent triangles in a grid, while also considering the various patterns they can represent in this distinct setting. As part of a broader exploration, this topic contributes to ongoing discussions around numerical triangles in a grid and serves as a model for other "Demonstrations Without Words" to combine art and mathematics. Neural networks with graph structure are highly versatile and apply to a variety of image and video processing tasks.  Despite this, there is a lack of flexible and scalable tools for developing and experimenting with these networks, as compared to traditional CNNs. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) interpreter that dynamically adjusts its parameters based on input size to optimize memory, time, and intermodule communication. This interpreter can run alongside the original module for real-time inference, allowing it to take advantage of cached intermediate results and reducing its memory usage fivefold. It also includes a function for building and modifying GNN models based on a given architecture, and includes sample use cases that demonstrate its effectiveness. Overall, the GNN interpreter enables the scalable development and debugging of graph neural networks. The cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 at z=0.28, previously classified as a system with multiple X-ray components, is studied to determine its structural properties in both the southern component (RXCJ0232.2-4420 South) and the main component (RXCJ0232.2-4420 North). By using King and beta elliptical models, we analyzed the surface brightness distribution of the two components, finding that the cluster consists of a single system composed of two substructures. We discovered that the distance between these substructures is approximately 1.5 Mpc (3.5 arcmin) and that they share a common redshift. A plot of galaxy distribution revealed a long, narrow structure aligned nearly east-west that contains multiple groups and galaxies, indicating a dynamic system with possible mergers. The merger history of the cluster is explored, including a history spanning 2-4 Gyr, and we suggest that the cluster may have undergone a recent major merger, likely with a mass ratio of 1-3:1, which could explain its complex structure and contribution to the formation of its southern substructure. This analysis also explores the evolution of the system and suggests that the cluster may have had a simple structure 1-2 Gyr ago but has since become more complex. We provide a timeline based on our findings and discuss the possible impact of the cluster's environment, as well as a possible candidate for the merger that could explain the cluster's structure. We have also examined the possible connection between the tangential richness of galaxies in the field of the cluster and the merger history of the cluster, and we have explored the possible effects of the merger on the dynamics and structure of the cluster. This analysis provides an understanding of the cluster's complex structure and its relationship to its tangential richness. We have also examined the possible effects of the merger on the dynamics and structure of the cluster. A companion paper provides further context and analysis by examining the substructure of the two cluster components in multiple wavelengths. The system with multiple X-ray components is now a valuable laboratory for studying the evolution of galaxy clusters and their structure. The recently introduced Legendre Memory Unit is a type of recurrent neural network specifically designed for sequence-to-sequence tasks and has been demonstrated to achieve high performance and efficient processing capabilities. A more advanced variant, the parallelized Legendre Memory Unit, was developed by replacing the original GMU component with its parallel-friendly counterpart, allowing for easier distribution of the model's internal state across multiple computing nodes. This more advanced model maintains the computational efficiency and memory advantages of the original LMU model while making it amenable to distributed and parallel training. As a result, the parallelized LMU can handle longer input sequences, resulting in significant improvements in processing speed. Experimentation with this model on the NMT benchmark dataset showed that it can achieve a high CAGR in processing efficiency, while maintaining a minimal reduction in overall accuracy. As the model's memory can be scaled up, it may offer a more efficient solution for handling long-form sequential data. Given the growing importance of processing large datasets in NLP and other related fields, this model presents a promising approach to this challenge. Recent experiments have made significant contributions to our understanding of beyond-the-standard-model physics by setting limits on the interactions between light hidden sector particles and standard model particles.  With ongoing and future experiments providing more restrictive limits, a new theory involving weakly-interacting dark matter has emerged as a strong contender to address the dark matter paradox.  This talk will examine recent and upcoming investigations into super-wimpy and co-annihilating dark matter, as well as other areas such as hidden U(1) fields and neutrinoless double beta decay.  Each of these areas will be explored with associated limits from mediators and dark matter in the eV to GeV mass range.  Hints of activity in these searches would be highly significant, offering a promising lead in the search for beyond-the-standard-model physics and a potential solution to the dark matter puzzle.  A particular emphasis will be placed on the potential role of fermionic and scalar mediators in these parity-breaking processes.  In addition, we will explore the potential implications of these beyond-the-standard-model physics scenarios for the proposed CUPID-Z experiment, which aims to increase limits on the Z-portal dark matter process by an order of magnitude.  This investigation is significant as dark matter in the Z-portal theory model is a strong competitor to the Higgs-portal theory model for explaining weakly-interacting dark matter.  A particular emphasis will be placed on the role of Z-portal dark matter in explaining the galactic center gamma-ray excess in the annual galactic circular anisotropy.  This excess refers to a 3.7 Sigma annual circular anisotropy excess in the 34-39 GeV mass range observed in the galactic center by the Advanced ALFA experiment.  The particular theory model being investigated in this work is one where a super-wimpy dark matter particle in the eV mass range co-annihilates with a 34-39 GeV mediator particle to form pairs of visible and invisible particles that contribute to the annual galactic circular anisotropy.  The particular mediator particle is a fermion or scalar that is a mix of standard model and hidden sector particles which couple to standard model particles via a very weak Yukawa interaction. In linguistic labeling games, the objective is to achieve consistent language use among players through limited exchanges. Prior research demonstrated that, in a fixed-setting model, the exchange process inevitably converges toward linguistic consistency. Building on this foundation, our study introduces a dynamic model where players are free to engage with one another, enabling a geographic distribution of interactions. Our research investigates linguistic exchange in this distributed setting and reveals that the likelihood of reaching linguistic consistency varies according to the underlying network structure of the player community. Specifically, our studies on random and targeted networks show that a more interconnected world tends to facilitate linguistic exchange and increases the likelihood of consistency among players. Furthermore, our linguistic labeling game model includes adjustable parameters that represent the degree of preference for clear communication and the significance of social connections. By adjusting these parameters, our studies also explore the resilience of linguistic exchange in diverse environments. Ultimately, our research suggests that linguistic exchange and its outcomes are shaped by the complex interplay of social preferences and geographic distribution of social interactions. The corresponding numerical methods employed in this study rely on the hybrid approach combining deterministic modeling of linguistic exchange processes and probabilistic representation of player communities. Our study specifically utilizes the finite-volume semi-discrete numerical technique for solving elliptic equations involved in linguistic exchange processes. In addition, our research incorporates the basin-homogenization approach for modeling migrant distribution among player communities. To assess the dynamic behavior of linguistic exchange processes in distributed settings, we employed the method of upper-lower solutions and monotone schemes. Our numerical studies were conducted using the finite-element method for solving elliptic equations in multiple dimensions, coupled with the first-order upwind scheme and its variants. Our results confirm that linguistic exchange processes can be classified into different types, ranging from stable to oscillatory or chaotic states, and that these patterns are influenced by the underlying social network structure. The corresponding numerical methods were thoroughly verified through convergence and stability analyses, demonstrating robust and efficient solutions to linguistic exchange problems in distributed settings. Furthermore, our research explored the social implications of linguistic dynamics by modeling language transitions as first-order reversible processes with meta-stable states. In a three-dimensional environment, our studies revealed that linguistic exchange can be influenced by the geometry of player communities, leading to diverse dynamic patterns, such as language transition mechanisms between stable states, oscillations between two states, and state transitions among multiple stable states. The corresponding numerical methods were also validated through convergence and stability analyses. Ultimately, our research suggests that linguistic exchange processes in complex distribution settings exhibit rich and diverse characteristics. PINN algorithms have demonstrated significant potential in solving complex partial differential equations (PDEs) by incorporating multiple constraints. However, the methods currently available often result in inaccurate predictions for scenarios involving intricate details or high-dimensional inputs. This inaccurateness is attributed to the spectral bias inherent in multilayer neural networks. This research explores the impact of using the Momentum optimization algorithm to mitigate spectral bias in PINN systems by introducing orthogonal initialization for the gradients at the data points. We test an adapted variant of the Adam optimization method, referred to as 'Momentum PINN' (M-PINN). Our experiments compare M-PINN with traditional PINN at integrating ordinary differential equations (ODMs) and validating our results with in-depth analytical examinations. The outcome of our investigation suggests that utilizing Momentum in PINN leads to a substantial decrease in the spectral bias, resulting in improved performance and accurate predictions for a range of complex IVPs and HPDPs. We also discover that M-PINN is capable of accurately predicting the White Lie derivative for a control problem involving a Riemann invariance. This development is accompanied by a theoretical justification for the spectral bias reduction by proving that M-PINN preserves the eigenvalues of the data gradients. We anticipate that this research will facilitate the use of the Momentum optimization method in PINN and other neural network-based algorithms aimed at solving PDEs. Blind image restoration, specifically deblurring and denoise, is a complex issue in image processing. To address these tasks, conventional methods typically rely on a few key parameters including the blurring kernel and noise standard deviation. However, in most cases, these parameters are unknown and must be estimated. Recent "plug and play" type models have made significant progress by incorporating variational regularizers that indirectly estimate these parameters. Nevertheless, there are limitations to the versatility of these prior models. This study presents a novel approach by utilizing kernel mixture models as regularizers, allowing for varied kernel choices and mixtures. Moreover, the expressive power of MOP models can be adjusted with a sparse prior assumption on the mixture coefficients. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach and its ability to adapt to diverse prior models by simply changing the types of kernels in the mixture. This paper introduces a new equation known as the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation (NUIYBE) and examines its connection to the associative Yang-Baxter equation (YBE). We show that the NUIYBE has two distinct sub-equations, which are the uniform and non-uniform associative Yang-Baxter equations (UIYBE and NUITYBE). Furthermore, each of these two equations has two different interpretations. The analysis focuses on bihomomorphisms that satisfy both UIYBE and NUIYBE, and we identify and categorize such bihomomorphisms in terms of their order and rank. Our study also includes the cases of uniform and non-uniform 2-adic Yang-Baxter equations (U2YBE and NU2YBE). In addition, by incorporating a parameter, we investigate the relationships between solutions to both NUIYBE and U2YBE, as well as between NUIYBE and NU2YBE. Finally, this paper outlines a method for categorizing different types of unitary solutions to these two uniform and non-uniform 2-adic Yang-Baxter equations (U2GE and N2GE). (The two-dimensional generalization in this context refers to homomorphisms of the form $a \otimes b$ where $a$ and $b$ are different variables). Formal verification is a critical phase in creating dependable software, and languages such as Hoare logic and predicate calculus serve as the groundwork for expressing its rules. The development of automated tools for assuring software code reliability has driven Hoare logic's adoption, and recent breakthroughs have successfully integrated logic and source code, enabling fully automated verification. Despite the significance of software programming in natural language, like English, and the existence of syntactically analyzed forms (e.g., SQL, Python code with type specifiers) enabling formal verification, no systematic approach has been developed for naturally expressed specifications, a crucial element of dependable software development. This research proposes a method for naturally expressed specifications, referred to as Natural Hoare Reasoning. It allows programmers to write dependable software by describing its safe modifications to code through English statements, which are analyzed for correctness, and specifies a robust reasoning framework incorporating a range of techniques. The study provides insight into its development and demonstrates its potential with a dependable search function employing relational data in Python. Distributed consensus is a fundamental process that allows multiple entities to agree on a common state despite network faults and diverse system requirements. Existing research has focused on creating algorithms suitable for specific use cases, such as self-stabilization and fail-invariant consensus. Although self-stabilizing algorithms are designed to withstand arbitrary initial conditions and reach a consensus state without relying on specific premises, failure of consensually active components can still cause issues. Our RCanopus system proposal addresses this by ensuring the robust continuation of failure-prone Canopus consensus for self-stabilizing systems, effectively providing a consensus layer for non-failural systems as well. To achieve this, we integrate a consensus layer with a failure handling mechanism, which automatically reconfigures when failures occur without overhauling the entire system. In addition to failures, we also developed a robust Canopus variant that can withstand Byzantine attacks, marking the first failure-prone consensus algorithm to do so. Our numerical analysis demonstrates the performance benefits of our proposed model, revealing that RCanopus can reduce average communication costs by up to three times compared to traditional self-stabilizing consensus approaches. Furthermore, our model allows for automatic detection and handling of diverse failure types, from simple node crashes to complex Byzantine attacks. Our testing protocol validates the accuracy of our analysis by comparing the results to those obtained from real-world implementations of RCanopus and its competitors. To facilitate the evaluation of different failure scenarios and consensus algorithms, we developed a failure simulation tool. Our real-world testing covered three distinct failure scenarios and two consensus algorithms, which revealed a notable difference in performance between the two options. Together, these results confirm that robust Canopus is an efficient and reliable consensus algorithm, capable of withstanding various failure types and non-byzantine attacks while providing optimal performance. The code for our failure simulation tool is available for further research purposes at https://github.com/tonyim/microgrid. Our testing protocol is documented at https. www.dropbox.com/COVID-Testing-Protocol.pdf. An extensive air-shower register of the highest-energy cosmic particles has been created with the help of the Pierre Auger Observatory. This register spans a 10-year period and encompasses 10 years of observations with the Sigma Auger Telescope. It features over 10 billion events with energies above 10^18.7 eV and provides comprehensive coverage of the full Southern Hemisphere sky. This register includes 10^19 particles that would have been recorded during 50 years of continuous monitoring. This study presents the register's results focusing on the most energetic particles and their energy distribution, as well as exploring relationships with incoming particle directions and air showers' top masses. These findings are compared to two popular models of the cosmic ray spectrum: one assuming Poisson distribution and the other based on a two-component model with a 5 sigma suppression around 57.7 eV. Additionally, the study examines connections between the energy of primary particles and water depth, distance from the equator, and aerial density, and discusses potential interrelations between these factors. No correlations with dates were identified during the 10-year data collection period. Lastly, the study discusses possible relationships between the highest-energy particles and Earth's magnetic field, as well as the characteristics of primary particles as hypothesized to be extremely energetic and rare nuclei. This study outlines prospects for future investigations and discusses supplementary methods to enhance understanding of the highest-energy particles and their byproducts. One such method involves utilizing the BAICata data system to analyze and managing extensive air-shower registers with the aid of the Auger Telescope. This system was also used to create a 10-year dataset for the Phi Auger Telescope. Together with the Sigma Auger Telescope, these tools enable simultaneous two-dimensional analysis of the highest-energy particles and their energy distributions with the help of the Auger Telescope. This study results in a comprehensive map of the highest-energy particles and their energy across 20 years of observations with the Sigma and Phi Auger Telescopes. This study also explores the most energetic particles as extreme outliers and their connections to events with energies below the GZK boundary. One such example is the 10^19.72 eV event with right ascension 13.69 and declination -45.11. No correlations were found between the energy of primary particles and their arrival directions, and these results are compared to two theoretical models of the cosmic ray spectrum. No 5 sigma suppression around 57.7 eV was observed near the kinematic boundary of the highest-energy particles as of 2021.

We introduce BayesOD, a novel, computationally efficient deep learning-based framework for quantifying prediction uncertainty in object detection tasks. This method builds on existing object detectors by adding a categorical probability distribution to the parameterization of a predictor network. This parameterization predicts an object as present with a given value for each spatial location on an image. A Bayesian inference procedure is then applied to yield the probability of an object's true class labels being present in each location. Our experimental findings with deep learning-based detectors on benchmark datasets demonstrate that BayesOD successfully assesses uncertainty in object detection accurately. We've proposed a novel method for forecasting traffic conditions.
Our approach involves analyzing short segments of roads at frequent intervals 
to identify patterns that persist on specific sections and then using these 
patterns to make predictions about future road segments.
By employing a deep learning model, which incorporates spatially
related information across multiple road sections, we've been able to 
significantly reduce the uncertainty associated with forecasting traffic 
conditions.
Our innovative method not only yields more accurate traffic forecasts 
compared to conventional prediction models, but also improves their overall 
clarity and efficiency. Furthermore, we've successfully adapted this 
methodology to several test cases spanning multiple cities located in 
the US, China, and Australia. We challenge the scientific community to 
foster more collaboration and data sharing to address the growing 
challenge of forecasting traffic conditions as cities continue to 
expanding and becoming more congested. We also provide access to our data 
and tools via a public repository located on the GitHub platform. 

The forecasting performance of our approach was evaluated across three 
test cases, which highlighted its ability to identify intricate patterns 
within data, achieve consistent forecasting accuracy, and obtain optimal 
prediction performance. Our results also comparison of our method with 
existing KNN and LSTM architectures demonstrated a 25% improvement in 
prediction performance. Additionally, the spatially aware self-attention 
model appeared to be particularly resilient to anomalies within the 
annotation dataset. We plan to further develop this methodological 
innovation to anticipate and forecast other forms of spatial data, 
such as air quality. The associated code can be accessed at the public 
GitHub repository located at: https://github.com/ashawkey/trafficforecast. The 
dataset can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashawkey/traffic_dataset. We 
intend to supplement this work by investigating alternative deep 
learning models for spatial forecasting and developing a distributed 
self-learning system for traffic prediction. The primary source code for 
this project can be found at: https://www.github.com.

This type of light beam allows us to link the atom-microphone interaction in a one-to-one correspondence during the excitation process. Notably, the pigeonhole effect is observed not only in the single-photon transition but also in the two-photon transition from the second energy level back to the ground state. Our research utilizes a single-atom Raman transition to verify the two-photon effect. Our experiments successfully demonstrate the probability of having both Raman photons inside a 2 $\mu$m wide "pigeonhole" in transversal modes with a high accuracy (error margin of 4%), and we find the average time for one photon to enter the "pigeole" to be 7.18 ms. These findings open the door for using transversal light beams in quantum physics experiments that require detecting extremely rare events, such as the simultaneous arrival of multiple particles at a single point in space. Recent research has yielded impressive results in universal feature extraction for graphs using GNNs, however the current models' shortcomings are mainly reflected in two key areas. Firstly, a linear combination of pyramid-like features fails to meet the complex task requirements, as substantial reduction in detail leads to feature loss, hindering performance. Secondly, the task-dependent structure learned by heuristically designed graph enhancement methods is unreliable. This paper proposes the UNILINK framework addressing these issues by employing a task-independent universal feature extraction module and a link reconnection mechanism with adaptable structure learning. The links are selected based on the task-independent feature extraction properties and structural integrity and then reconnected through local structure encoding and node relation merging. The framework first applies a task-independent feature extraction module to capture primary structure information and then employs a link reconnection mechanism to introduce task-specific details. The UNILINK framework differentiates itself from current models with its lightweight structure, efficient computation, and adaptable task-specific details. The experiments reveal the UNILINK framework surpasses current benchmarks in performance on multiple tasks. The framework source code is available at https://github.com/ziplab/UNILINK. In recent years, numerous techniques have been employed to minimize the negative effects of differential privacy on low-dimensional matrix approximation methods. Although several methods such as noise-based and differential privacy-aware low-rank matrix techniques have been explored, there is still a pressing need for comprehensive algorithms that ensure low-dimensional matrix fulfillment while maintaining differential privacy. To address this gap, this research introduces the Huber framework, a novel approach leveraging the Huber loss function, to derive private low-rank matrix estimates that fulfill the Huber criterion. Moreover, this research demonstrates that the Huber framework is compatible with existing private low-rank matrix methods, such as the sparse eigenvalue problem and the noisy low-rank matrix method, to enhance the robustness of differential privacy in low-dimensional matrix approximation. To validate the Huber framework, two noise-based low-rank matrix fulfillment algorithms were designed and tested, one incorporating the sparse eigenvalue problem and the other the noisy low-rank matrix method. As a result, the findings indicate that the Huber framework offers superior low-rank matrix fulfillment performance, as well as more accurate and precise low-rank matrix reconstruction, especially when applied to noisy datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this research provides the first evaluation of the Huber framework for low-dimensional matrix approximation methods, offering promising applications in machine learning and data analysis. Ultimately, the Huber framework has the potential to significantly advance and improve the low-rank matrix fulfillment methods in machine learning and data analysis. The research's key technical aspects are documented in a new manuscript titled "Introducing the Huber framework for differentially private low-rank matrix fulfillment." The authors conducted an original analysis of the noise-based low-rank matrix approximation methods' effectiveness and provided two new algorithmic designs, Huber-NL and Huber-CR, to demonstrate the low-rank matrix fulfillment method's differentially private capability as proven by the Huber loss function's differential privacy fulfillment guarantee. The research's key findings are further discussed in a new study titled "Differential privacy in low-rank matrix approximation methods: A study on noise-based low-rank matrix approximation algorithms." A new framework for understanding dust interaction in space is presented, combining existing information on dust types, composition, and behavior. Typically, a three-component model consists of large solid particles (astrodust) and two types of carbon-based molecular complexes (PAHs and larger VOCs) to describe space polarization and absorption properties. Based on recent analysis findings, the following updates are made to the model: A higher percentage of small PAHs compared to large VOCs (ratio of 3.2) is suggested, and the combined mass of both types of carbon-based components is approximately 100-1000 times smaller than the mass of astrodust particles. Additionally, the relationship between grain sizes and optical properties is analyzed, and a correlation is established between the size of astrodust particles and space polarization properties, and the PAH-based component's polarization properties in different radiation environments. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of space interaction and provide a starting point for modeling Earth's atmospheric conditions. This research focuses on the solvability and computational complexity of the $k$-Maximum Clicks problem, a variant of the Lights Out game. This problem involves finding a sequence of at most $k$ operations that maximizes the lights being turned on simultaneously. A few initial investigations are conducted: defining the problem as NP-complete, establishing its connection to the Maximum Independent Set problem, and exploring its relationship with the Maximum Common Edge Color Matching problem. Additionally, we examine whether $k$-MC is solvable in polynomial time for specific values of $k$, such as $k=2$ and $k=3$. We also investigate the related $k$-MC-Deux problem and derive a lower time complexity bound for this variant. Furthermore, we outline potential future research directions in this area. By formulating the task as a variational model with four core equations, including edge detection, image partitioning, color matching, and image refinement, this approach tackles two critical issues - image segmentation and image restoration - in a single step. Leveraging advanced mathematical techniques, such as gap function method, multiple scalarizing, and optimization methods, we convert the task into a minimum-energy problem subject to multiple constraints. Expanding the system to include an additional Kirchhoff current, we use advanced numerical methods to solve the resulting nonlinear system of equations. Our approach includes developing edge detection maps, solving the Bassin algorithm, and using the alternating direction method to solve the transformed minimum-energy problem. Our method achieves impressive results on a range of challenging datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation and image restoration accuracy. We investigate theoretical models of optical and acoustic modes within oxide perovskites. Their vibrational spectrum can be described by opposing forces of light and phonon wave propagation, leading to a unique phenomenon where the speed of phonon wave propagation depends on the amplitude of the laser stimulation. Diverging behavior is observed between geometric phonons and those with typical anharmonicity. A critical threshold exists beyond which the material becomes insensible to its crystal structure. Our analysis of the dynamic dielectric constant and the observation of discrete absorption peaks confirm that the state governed by light is characterized as a solid but weakly dissipative medium. A new category of functional materials, capable of significant adjustments to their vibrational structure and controlled by external light, is proposed. These materials could be utilized in a wide range of applications, including nonlinear optics, photonics, laser technology, and bio-medical fields. Our approach provides a foundation for designing novel photon and electron devices with adjustable band gaps. A new and promising direction is opened in the development of materials with adjustable phonon structures. A potential approach to creating stable structures of atomic scale in nanotechnology and the development of stable materials with adjustable phonon structure is proposed. A description of the underlying nature of geometric phonons within the context of light-phonon interaction as the primary mechanism is provided. A theoretical model is presented to explain how the unique properties of geometric phonons arise from the symmetries of the perovskite structure and the principle of light-phonon interaction. A first principle investigation of the central frequency and the anharmonicity of geometric phonons in BaTiO3 and PZT is conducted. Our findings provide insights into the causes of supercriticality and explain why geometric phonons in BaTiO3 and PZT do not exhibit strong anharmonicity. We identify the critical behavior of geometric phonons under adiabatic conditions and propose an approach to observing geometric phonons through x-ray scattering. Our investigation of light-phonon interaction in a centrosymmetric material reveals the underlying nature of geometric phonons. Our approach provides a measurable indicator to distinguish between harmonic and anharmonic behaviors. A theoretical model is developed to explain how to adjust the unique properties of geometric phonons through external stress. A device that utilizes stress to control geometric phonons is proposed. Our investigation provides a strategic framework for developing materials with adjustable geometric phonons. Anomaly detection in time-series data is a crucial task that typically uses distance or similarity measures to identify data points that deviate from their peers. Most existing methods rely on a fixed radius or threshold to find anomalies, but they have significant drawbacks as they cant adapt to varying radius values and are heavily influenced by outliers. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel method that accurately and efficiently identifies anomalies by constructing a closeness graph in the metric space. This graph separates normal data points from anomalies, and its construction is scalable for real-world applications. Our proposed method compares favorably with existing approaches on both synthetic and real-world datasets. It outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by achieving 2.5% higher precision and 1.1% higher recall on the Google dataset and 9.4% higher precision and 4.5% higher recall on the Amazon dataset. Additionally, our method demonstrates a significant performance improvement, running 5-12 times faster than the top-performing baseline method. Hexahedral meshes hold significant value in various scientific and engineering fields for the accurate simulation and visualization of complex physical phenomena. Unlike other types of unstructured meshes, hexahedral meshes possess distinct advantages, such as efficiently handling different boundary conditions and efficiently reducing the time spent in calculations, especially in fields like numerical methods for partial differential equations. However, hexahedral mesh generation is a highly complex task requiring specialized techniques to create high-quality meshes from given volumes, especially when it comes to volumes with intricate features. Isotropic hexahedral mesh generation is a highly researched topic with numerous papers addressing its different aspects like superlinear convergence and efficient algorithms, but there is limited research on creating detailed and smooth meshes with high spatial accuracy. In this study, the authors introduce an innovative approach to hexahedral mesh generation that simulates the smooth process of dividing cells into smaller ones, using the Laplacian-based approach, and maintaining the overall smoothness of the mesh. Another area of improvement in hexahedral mesh generation is the efficient integration of different data sets to create detailed and smooth meshes. To address this, the authors introduce innovative efficient algorithms to decompose and rearrange cells based on different data fields and create detailed and smooth meshes with different levels of spatial refinement, up to 58 times, using the same basic hexahedral structure. These algorithms utilize the smooth process of dividing cells into smaller ones and the ability to create detailed and smooth meshes with different levels of spatial refinement, up to 58 times, to efficiently handle various data sets and create detailed and smooth meshes. Detailed results show the authors' algorithm's ability to create the complex details required to accurately simulate the fluid dynamics of complex systems from the detailed and smooth meshes generated using the introduced algorithms. Discovering relations between entities is a crucial, yet difficult task often encountered in information extraction. This study aims to improve relation discovery by employing connection prediction in knowledge graphs. Existing relation discovery methods primarily rely on raw sentence data, whereas this work integrates data on the subjects and objects within knowledge graphs to inform relation extraction. A novel approach has been developed, called KBCP, which predicts subject-to-object relationships within these graphs. By combining KBCP with existing relation discovery models, comprehensive evaluation results demonstrate substantial performance enhancements on benchmark datasets. Specifically, our hybrid models result in up to a 19% increase in F1 score compared to standalone relations, as seen on the Wikipedia50K dataset. Furthermore, experiments conducted on the more extensive Wikipedia100K dataset also yield significant improvements, with hybrid models achieving a score 34% higher than their standalone counterparts. These significant findings highlight the potential of leveraging knowledge graphs to enhance relation discovery, a technique especially valuable in large, comprehensive graph datasets. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/fnogas/KBCP. Our technique relaxes the requirement for topic balance, a notable advantage in relation extractions involving less common topics. By training the model to connect subjects and objects across the graph, it can often relate a subject to an object from a different topic, even if the topic balance is not initially apparent. This capability makes the KBCP technique particularly useful in scenarios where data is heavily distributed across various topics, as the model's ability to connect subjects and objects across the graph can inform relation extraction more effectively than traditional topic-balanced approaches. The model's performance on the Wikipedia50K dataset is exemplary, with an F1 score of 0.7273, while demonstrating substantial gains in relation extraction when applied to the more extensive Wikipedia100K dataset. The accompanying code at https://github.com/fnogas/KBCP was used to achieve these results. The underlying distribution of the subjects can often inform relation extraction, as the model's ability to connect subjects and objects across the graph can reflect underlying topics more effectively than traditional topic-balanced approaches. The accompanying code at https://github.com/fnogas/KBCP was used to achieve these results. The technique's adaptability in scoping was evaluated by training the model to predict connections for a subset of subjects, allowing it to learn and preserve entity topics more effectively. When evaluating images of objects, humans respond more strongly to those that represent living entities such as animals, as opposed to inanimate objects like cars. Our investigation reveals that this distinction arises from the interplay of various factors, including an object's movement, its level of biological complexity and the presence of a face. To better understand this distinction, we developed a system that identifies animacy levels, ranging from non-living to large animals, and found that participants easily make distinctions at different animacy levels but struggle with finer distinctions. Furthermore, using fMRI, we identified a specific region in the visual cortex known as the lateral occipital complex that responds specifically to images of large animals but not smaller creatures or inanimate objects. Our findings suggest that ventral temporal processing of images of objects, including those that are living or non-living, relies on a hierarchical series of animacy arrangements. They also highlight the limitations of automated image recognition systems, which tend to excel at distinguishing between large animacy categories such as'mammals' but struggle to pinpoint more specific classes like 'birds' and'reptiles'. Our work provides insights into the underlying visual system arrangements that enable humans to differentiate between images of objects, including those that are living or non-living. High-order numerical methods face difficulties due to their sensitivity in calculations and lack of stability when dealing with small perturbations. They often benefit from techniques like stabilization or regularization to ensure stability and accuracy. For the context of partial differential equations and multidimensional simulations, an alternative approach exists in developing specialized filters that preserve the solution's properties. This work develops and evaluates a new convex optimization-based filter, referred to as the COF, which maintains key characteristics of the solution, such as its smoothness and spatial structure, by minimizing a specially designed cost function. This innovative approach results in the preservation of important features like notches, corners, and even complex geometric details. Moreover, due to its uniqueness, the solution obtained is often more robust and free from spurious oscillations, achieving this through the enforcement of the Eulers-Poincare system's optimality conditions. To test the effectiveness of the COF, it is applied to two complex problems, including the analysis of a circular membrane with a notch at its center and a more intricate geometric calculation, involving the interaction of a surface-to-air mass transfer process and the Von Karman vortex street. Both simulations enunciate the benefits and capabilities of the proposed COF, confirming its potential to deliver accurate results in the context of the described frameworks. This work is further supported by the open-source code, available at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/tonyodeh/COF_journals. This code can be used both for the simulation described in this study and for the development of new applications, with a pre-built toolkit allowing for easy and user-friendly processing. This study envisions that the proposed COF may be adapted to address additional challenges in the context of the described frameworks, contributing to the advancement of the field. One of the suggested avenues for future research includes the development of an automated algorithm for the determination of the threshold used in the COF, via a maximum a posteriori optimization approach, at the beginning of each time step. This contribution is envisioned to deliver more efficient results, especially in the context of time-dependent simulations, by reducing the current limitation of the threshold value ($10^{-8}$) on a relatively standard machine. This study envisions that the proposed maximum a posteriori threshold-optimized COF may be adapted to address related challenges in the context of the described numerical frameworks. Moreover, the results presented enunciate the need for further research aimed at the development of a unified theory explaining the behavior of stabilization techniques, which may be the subject of a future study. We identified a new phase in MAXI J1535-571's type-C quasi-periodic oscillation variability, characterized by prominent and dynamic patterns that emerged during the 2017-2018 outburst. This new phase, called the corona phase, was distinguished by a sudden increase in count rates and the development of complex structures in the soft and hard gamma-ray bands. Our Insight-HXMT observations revealed that the corona phase was marked by a series of fluctuation harmonics with a correlation of 0.9, indicating a coherent system, and a high hard-to-soft spectrum, indicating inverse Comptonization as the primary mechanism. This phase was associated with a geometrically complex corona and a highly excited accretion flow, consistent with a corona-driven accretion flow during the corona phase. Moreover, our Insight-HXMT observations in the hard band showed that the corona phase was characterized by a spectrum that could be fit by an exponential or power-law tail, suggesting the presence of non-thermal particles. This could be due to a corona boundary where radiation pressure causes a acceleration of particles or the existence of a small geometrically collimated jet. Our study shows that the corona phase in MAXI J1535-571's variability can be used to probe the outer boundaries of the corona. Furthermore, our observations of the corona phase in other sources, such as the 2019-2020 outburst in MAXI J1745-25, provide insight into the universal nature of this phenomenon. At last, our study shows that the concept of a dynamic corona, defined as a changing geometric or physical structure, can explain the variability in type-C quasi-periodic oscillations in various sources, implying that this phenomenon may be ubiquitous in black hole X-ray binaries. This could be explained by a black hole undergoing a persistent, accretion-driven jet due to a stable disk-jet interaction, where the jet can interact with the accretion disk to drive quasi-periodic oscillations. This model is supported by data from Insight-HXMT, as the total flux of soft and hard gamma-ray variability in MAXI J1535-571 corresponds to a fundamental frequency of 0.25 Hz. This could be further studied in other sources to confirm its applicability. In multi-agent learning (MAL), the social transfer of knowledge is a common issue.
Malicious agents often undermine social trust by engaging in untrustworthy behavior,
while seeking transfer enablement from a kind partner fosters social trust and
motivates cooperative behavior. Current model-based algorithms and their variants
often ignore the agent's need for transfer enablement and fail to address their
motivation for cooperation. As a result, they tend to be overly competitive and
lacking in consistency. Our proposed framework, social inherent motivation of
transfer enablement (SITE), is a multi-agent learning framework designed to
address the motivation for transfer enablement and foster a trustworthy social
environment. SITE introduces a reliable response mechanism to address an agent's
cooperative intentions by providing consistent and trustworthy decisions.
Under conditions of uncertainty, SITE's reliable response mechanism helps to
guard against the vulnerability to malicious agents while motivating cooperative
behavior among partners. Our experiments demonstrate SITE's superior performance
compared to state-of-the-art models and its capacity to address an agent's
motivation for transfer enablement and foster a trustworthy social environment.

We've developed a novel technique for identifying unknown substances under real-time visual input. The method trains an artificial intelligence model to distinguish between real-world materials by simulating how it would learn through interaction and visual feedback. This substance identification method achieves optimal performance with the fewest possible measurements by emulating a curious AI that seeks maximum information to minimize confusion. To optimize the learning process, we prioritize the AI's ability to recognize its own errors in identification and understand how input data contributes to resolving uncertainties. To enhance generalization, we ensured the AI learns universal patterns applicable to any possible input by supplementing the training process with fundamental principles of how substances interact physically. This approach not only improves generalization but also helps the AI to prioritize learning tasks based on their physical relevance. We validate the effectiveness of this method in identifying a wide range of common substances solely by their visual appearance. The corresponding source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andreabacci/ce4id. We introduce a novel method for detecting regional feature matches without using a detector, which relies on a specialized transformer that looks along parallel lines to find corresponding regions' features. By scanning in parallel and comparing features along each line, our method, called LoFTR, is efficient both in computation and data preparation. It can find matches for any given image pair quickly and has the ability to adapt its level of precision. We tested LoFTR on both artificial and real-world problems, achieving good results in both cases. In comparison to existing methods, LoFTR excelled on several metrics and was particularly well-performing when there were significant differences in the images being matched. Furthermore, LoFTR was used to demonstrate new techniques for using both individual and group information when matching features, while also allowing for more accurate prediction of geometric transformations. Code for LoFTR is available at https://github.com diffuseprob/LoFTR.

This study proposes a novel decentralized scheme for managing energy consumption in smart grids that effectively imposes load reduction orders by leveraging energy consumption modeling and real-time billing of consumers' energy usage surges above predetermined limits. To minimize consumption variability and better align energy demand with available energy supply and network capacity, the proposed system includes an advanced demand response mechanism. Initially, an optimization model identifies an optimal energy consumption schedule for a group of consumers while adhering to supply constraints, and each consumer's scheduled energy usage is compared with actual consumption to determine potential load reduction targets. A non-convex optimization problem and a linear programming solution are used to calculate the optimal energy consumption schedule and determine load reduction opportunities. To ensure the feasibility of the scheduled energy consumption, a smart charger manages charging in accordance with the scheduled energy usage until a certain time, known as the sliding window. At the end of the sliding window, any charged energy is adjusted to ensure the initially planned energy consumption is maintained. Furthermore, real-time billing ensures adherence to the initially planned energy consumption, and a game-theoretic approach solves the non-convex problem to determine load reduction targets. Consequently, the proposed system results in feasible and optimized energy consumption profiles for all consumers within the smart grid network. The effectiveness of the proposed scheme is evaluated using comprehensive numerical simulations of various smart charger solutions. In a modified general relativity known as the Rastall theory, our study examines Hawking radiation from charged black string solutions. As a result, our analysis indicates that when considering gravitational effects in the vicinity of black string strings, Hawking radiation is suppressed. However, the study shows that Hawking radiation is unaffected by the modified source term. We obtained these findings through a semi-classical model derived from the Horowitz-Podolsky prescription, taking into account a backdoor effect and a semi-classical black hole boundary. Additionally, our study reveals that Hawking radiation is suppressed more in the case of charged black string solutions than in the case of charged black holes. This suppression is attributed to two factors: first, the study confirms that gravitational effects in the vicinity of black holes diminish their horizon areas, thereby reducing the number of degrees of freedom. The study of extremely metal-poor stars, particularly those with very low metal content, relies on identifying these stars in the field. We examine various measures of word morphology, including Optimal String Representation, S-entropy, intrinsification, ambigraf, path length, and connections, to understand their relationships. Among these, a group related to intrinsification and ambigraf shows a strong correlation, while another, consisting of path length and connections, does not. This discovery leads us to suggest that intrinsification and ambigraf, which capture words' internal structures, are effective measures of morphology. We then provide a linear model to explain the correlation, linking it to the word's frequency distribution. Our findings ultimately support the use of a hybrid method combining multiple character-based metrics to authenticate a word's morphology. Additionally, this approach enables the creation of a universal scale to quantify morphology, similar to those developed by Zipf and Bauer, to analyze language evolution. We apply this method to English, German, and Russian, and the results indicate that while English exhibits distinct characteristics, such as evenly distributed vowel combinations in monosyllabic words, its morphology has not significantly changed over time. Conversely, incorporating character frequencies as a factor, our analysis of English, German, and Russian reveals that languages exhibit frequent vowel combinations but also display tendencies toward reduction, as seen in the use of 'u' in English, as well as enlargement, as seen in the use of 'ch', 'ch', and'sh' in Russian. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that in languages exhibiting a reduced tendency, their morphology often increases, as does the use of 'u' in Russian and 'qu' in English during their respective enlargements. We utilize the created scale to quantify the morphology of English, German, and Russian at different points in time, demonstrating that English exhibits steadily increasing morphology over time. In contrast, German's morphology has not changed, while Russian's morphology has fluctuated, becoming more intricate in the 20th century. We also identify periodic enlargements and reductions in the use of certain consonant combinations, as well as possible connections to other words sharing the same root. Finally, our analysis offers potential explanations for these observed language developments, as well as the effectiveness of certain character-based metrics in capturing words' internal structures. In doing so, we highlight the importance of frequency as a unifying factor in language evolution. The approach is considered from both corpus-based and theoretical perspectives, providing a foundation for further research on authenticity in the context of morphology. We also release the related data and code for public access at https://github.com/aleksander-raznitski

Recent developments in deep learning methods such as autonomous feature extraction (AFE) have achieved high accuracy in various medical image classification tasks, particularly when using MRI and CT scans. Recent fast AFE approaches were proposed to speed up MRI-based classification, utilizing a two-stage process: the first stage involves a rank-reduced PCA transformation followed by a low-rank matrix multiplication, and the second stage includes a sparse linear combination of activations. We have adapted a fast AFE method for use with binary sensors and sensors with multiple values, and developed M-ar-K-Fast, a compact version of the fast AFE technique. M-ar-K-Fast achieves compactness by replacing the rank-reduced PCA transformation with multiplicative autoencoders. We evaluated M-ar-Fast on 12 datasets from various sources and compared its performance to the original method and an improved version that incorporates color augmentation. The results show that M-ar-K-Fast performs similarly or better in terms of accuracy, while significantly improving compactness and outperforming the color augmentation approach in terms of accuracy and compactness. M-ar-K-Fast has been made available on GitHub under the MIT license. We have also conducted a comprehensive ablation study, analyzing the contributions of each method and combining them to introduce novel approaches. The experiments indicate that the key component responsible for the method's compactness and accuracy is the multiplicative autoencoder, which captures key features, and the sparse linear combination, which effectively combines important features. Notably, the method's accuracy is enhanced when using multiplicative autoencoders in conjunction with two or more key features. When trained on MRI datasets, the proposed method's accuracy rivals that of state-of-the-art MRI classification techniques. A significant number of online advertising auctions are held each day, primarily in private settings, where only a specific number of bidders participate and bid on a given ad slot in each market. Many real-world auctions are plagued by a problem known as budget exhaustion, where bidders rapidly deplete their budgets due to the high demand, thus limiting their potential opportunities to make profits. To tackle this issue and maximize long-term revenues, we develop an innovative bidding solution based on optimal dynamic programming for a specific display advertising scenario. Our method takes into account a key constraint - a limited budget - and incorporates a crucial factor: the potential of winning auctions in the future. We establish specific conditions to ensure the existence of solutions and provide a practical, efficient solution that can be applied in complex, continuous auction environments. Our numerical tests confirm that our method outperforms other popular bidding techniques, yielding higher long-term revenues while ensuring a reasonable chance of success in auctions. Furthermore, we extend our approach to address another critical issue - the uncertainty associated with estimating the demand distributions and future auction prices. We introduce a novel risk-aware bounding technique to establish upper and lower limits on expected revenue, and then determine a suitable range of bids. Our method is validated by comparing its performance with human-generated bids and a leading automatic bidding system. Experimental results reveal that our approach successfully yields more accurate and profitable bids, and is even preferred by advertisers over human-bidded campaigns. Overall, our method aims to balance revenue and campaign success rates through a novel bidding strategy. We hope that our research will inspire the development of future research directions. A prominent paradigm in reinforcement learning continues to be reward learning, where a suitable reward function is chosen based on a provided task description. However, reward functions are often difficult to specify in line with the task description, leading to a rewarding (no pun intended) solution - sample approximation. By leveraging neural networks and data from the environment, reward learning can adapt to complex tasks. Nevertheless, this method is time-consuming and may not suit tasks requiring precise domain knowledge. In this study, a more efficient approach called VSRCL is proposed. VSRCL utilizes a teacher-student model to categorize possible reward functions based on the task description and then applies policy evaluation to distill these categories. As decision-making autonomy in algorithms grows, the need for user understanding is reduced, but this only holds true for algorithms that are easy to comprehend. The concept of interpretability has become clear: algorithms must be understandable by both humans and the systems they themselves were trained on. Theoretical models of human cognition are essential in assessing this, and we introduce the Cognitive Complexity of an algorithm, measured by the depth of the associated human model's mental representation. This depth is quantified as the number of key components involved. The proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to any algorithm written in any programming language, and we demonstrate its use by applying it to clustering, random forests, and deep learning models. The framework highlights the role of meta-interpretability, which is the ability of an algorithm to recognize and explain its own internal decision-making processes, whether through self-awareness or external guidance. The need for meta-interpretability is thus the difference between the algorithm's understandability in isolation and when its decision-making processes are clearly defined. The proposed framework's main weakness is the subjectivity involved in assessing the depth of human models, and we suggest ways to mitigate this through the use of cognitive diversity in human teams. The final section discusses various potential applications of this framework, such as assessing the understandability of algorithms used in critical domains like medicine and the impact of cognitive biases in human-machine collaboration. The potential uses include measuring the return on investment for understanding human-centric AI systems, diagnosing understandable but underperforming algorithms, and evaluating the safety of complex human-machine partnerships. In this research, a velocity distribution with a fixed value for the average cross-section is called the fixed average cross-section (FAC) distribution. We identified a previously unknown category of FAC distributions characterized by a fixed average speed and defined a method to broaden this category. We broadened the fixed momentum (FM) distribution, another established FAC family, using FM-fitted gamma (FG) distributions. This led to two parameter families, FCC1 and FCC2, each with five distinct sub-families, consisting of nine new distributions. We compared each sub-family with its corresponding FM distribution, using mean cross-sections, mean energies, mean projectile ranges, and average stopping powers as criteria. Our analysis showed that the FCC1 and FCC2 distributions have the potential to provide better conditions for the generation of narrow synchrotron beams. Furthermore, the FCC1 and FG sub-families, with gamma > 1, may be more suitable for the creation of intense ion beams. We also observed that the FCC1 and FCC2 distributions can improve on existing polyenergetic distributions in this regard, while producing faster mean energies and projectiles, as well as increased charges, may offer advantages in certain applications. We analyzed the theoretical and practical uses of the newly discovered FACs and suggested generating these distributions experimentally. Our research extends the scope of FAC distributions, potentially leading to various applications in this category. Our findings indicate that the FCC1 and FCC2 distributions have the potential to create useful beam conditions for various scientific and technological purposes. Our method for broadening established FAC distributions can be applied in the future to generate new, potentially useful distributions. Furthermore, the production of FCC1 and FCC2 beams could mark the beginning of a new category of such distributions. Our analysis also indicates that the FCC1 and FCC2 distributions have the potential to be used in particle and nuclear physics, as well as in other fields. Our research at the fixed average cross-section (FAC) level has been extensive, allowing for the discovery of new distributions that may have valuable applications in physics and other fields. Our work at the fixed momentum (FM) level has led to the creation of two parameter families, consisting of nine new FACs, each with five sub-families, potentially expanding the scope of FM distribution conditions. The comprehension of everyday knowledge, shared by typical individuals with one another, is an essential aspect of human communication yet consistently poses challenges for artificial systems. Addressing this, COMET-ATOMIC 2020 is the upgraded version of a network initially introduced in 2018, offering an extensive, formally defined collection of atomic factual knowledge, carefully handpicked from existing datasets to showcase diverse everyday facts. Compared to its predecessor, COMET-ATOMIC 2020 exhibits significant advancements in three primary areas: increased language diversity, improved language precision, and substantially enhanced language generalization. The dataset's high quality, accuracy, and breadth make it suitable for training both symbolic and neural-based common sense knowledge acquisition systems, thus enabling it to be a valuable resource for evaluating such systems and facilitating comparisons. By utilizing advanced age and metallicity indicators, we investigated multiple star populations found in this cluster. Consistent with previous research, we identified four distinct metallicity segments within the cluster, spanning a metallicity range from -1.56 to -1.73 and supporting a multi-generational population of stars. Two of the metallicity segments (-1.56 and -1.68, as well as -1.68 and -1.73) were found to contain stars, with the metal richest segment consisting solely of horizontal-branch stars. This distribution of metallicity segments matches those observed in other heavy populations within the same region, such as M22 and 47 Tuc. Understanding the distribution of metallicity segments within globular clusters may provide valuable insights into their formation mechanisms. Consequently, the catalog can serve as a versatile tool not only for assessing an object's appearance but also for determining its proper orientation.  Furthermore, the proposed DIC method facilitates a range of applications, including generating dynamic product views, identifying object orientations, and creating character animations from images captured from various angles. Through experimental evaluations, I highlight the advantages of my proposed DIC method and demonstrate its superiority over alternative methods.  For instance, the results of a user study indicate that images generated using the proposed DIC method are more convincing and of higher quality than those produced using existing techniques. The proposed DIC method significantly enhances the overall visual impact of the generated images, thereby effectively conveying the dynamics of the underlying objects. In contrast, the proposed DIC method produces images in which the local and global transformations are seamlessly integrated. This process can be represented as an inverse problem where the timing and character of a reflected impulse train are estimated based on collected data. This proposed technique is uncomplicated and efficient, allowing it to operate at very fast speeds, outperforming existing techniques both in realistic simulations and with actual data. In modeling real-world scenarios as non-linear dynamical systems, the issue of predictive uncertainty in reinforcement learning becomes amplified, as point forecasts often fall short of reality. This leads to a major flaw: failing to convey the range of possible future states, also known as the prediction interval. This type of uncertainty quantification in reinforcement learning has long been neglected in the field. This paper tackles the challenge of forecasting equilibrium states in linear dynamic systems through the use of fixed point networks, which are based on the concept of linear regression. By leveraging the properties of Markov perfect equilibria, we demonstrate how to train a neural network to predict multiple step ahead equilibria and explore the potential of using such models in the context of prediction and defense against attacks. Furthermore, our experimental results show the significant advantages of fixed point networks over traditional methods, such as cross-validation, in terms of uncertainty quantification. We propose a straightforward statistical approach to evaluate causal relationships
between multiple variables. Our methodology is grounded in two key conditions:
the reliance of an outcome variable on one or more other variables, and the
existence of instances where at least one of these variables does not affect the outcome. 
Building on existing ideas, specifically the Weak Law of Large Numbers and
Fano's inequality, we develop a statistical method to examine multi-variable
causal relationships initially for binary variables and then more complex cases with continuous variables. 
An important benefit of our approach is its ability to identify interconnected
causal relationships among high-dimensional data. As a result, we provide new
insights into the asymptotic behavior of an important metric, the mutual information
independent of an additional variable, in sequences of high dimensional random
vectors. 
Our method is demonstrated through its application in various fields such as genetics, astronomy, and neural science, and we compare its performance to other existing techniques. 
Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of our approach to two significant problems in astronomy, namely the search for gravitational waves in N-dimensional signal data and the non-random distribution of Fast Radio Burst events across the sky. 
Using our approach, we also examine the complexity of relationships among different areas of the brain, revealing a hierarchical structure with higher correlations within the frontal cortex. 
In addition, we make the first attempt to identify the causal structure of relationships among genetic variables associated with particular diseases, revealing a significant connection between the Hilbert-Samelson signature and the logical expressions in probabilistic logic. 
All our results have been verified through publicly accessible databases and open-source code are available online at https://github.com/andreaballin/causal-analysis.
