Llinear time-invariant (LTI) systems are fundamental in modeling numerous processes across engineering, physics, and biology. LTI systems form the basis for nearly all control systems and offer a straightforward framework for modeling and predicting system behavior. However, in many cases, this simplicity is compromised by the presence of covert attacks that seek to manipulate or destroy the system. Most current methods for addressing such threats rely on the ability to observe the system at will, a scenario that may not apply in real-world situations where stealth attacks are a concern. In this paper, we develop a novel predictor for LTI systems under covert threats. Our approach recognizes that the adversary's impact can be transferred between system states, a key factor in determining the minimum number of observations required to prevent devastating attacks. This fundamental discovery enabled us to design a predictive model with minimal observational requirements, ultimately resulting in the most efficient solution available at the time of publication. Moreover, our method effectively balances the trade-off between maintaining the integrity of observations and effectively preventing stealth attacks. Our approach initially utilizes a data-driven method to determine the observational requirements necessary for a given level of threat protection. Subsequently, a specialized recursive algorithm is employed to estimate the system states and detect covert attacks in real-time. This integrated framework provides the basis for an effective predictive surveillance system. This method effectively handles instances of limited observational visibility and is versatile, applicable to a wide variety of real-world scenarios. Furthermore, our approach offers flexibility, allowing the user to customize the level of threat protection and observational requirements. In this study, we investigate the application of our method to the realm of gene regulation, a highly complex and high-stakes field where the concepts apply. This application of the method is supported by numerical experiments demonstrating the method's utility in this domain. This work is accompanied by an extensive supplementary online resource containing additional details of the method's implementation and application in the gene regulation field, along with supporting code and gene regulation datasets. This resource is publicly accessible and can be utilized by researchers and practitioners looking to adapt the method to various other fields and contexts. Ultimately, the method has far-reaching implications, a key takeaway from our work. Firstly, the method effectively addresses the concept of necessary observations required to prevent devastating stealth attacks in real-world scenarios. Secondly, the method offers a practical implementation of the fundamental observational requirements we previously determined to be necessary. Current studies on abstractive summarization have made significant advancements, focusing primarily on either limited or extended datasets in English. A notable exception is the unsupervised Graph-Aware Summarization of Text (GAST), which was applied to the complex case of multi-source, multilingual summaries. In this context, we introduce a new dataset consisting of eight languages representing three Indian languages, as well as language pairs, to facilitate the creation of a novel GAST variety (GAE-ISumm) designed for intricate Indian language summaries. Furthermore, we introduce a new diversity metric that gauges the variation of sentence similarity within a summary. Experimental results demonstrate that GAE-ISumm surpasses GAST in handling complex Indian language summaries, with GAE-ISumm also outperforming existing unsupervised models in quality and similarity to the gold summaries. Notably, human evaluations show that GAE-ISumm is comparable to supervised models in fluency and significantly surpasses them in preserving the original document content. We release the Indian language summarization dataset and GAE-ISumm source code for the benefit of the NLP community. This research is available on arXiv. \url{https://arxiv.org/under-submit}. We also demonstrate the equivalence of categories between the S-rings of Noether type and monoids with partial actions, thereby generalizing a previous theorem. Furthermore, to illustrate the broader applicability of our results, we provide examples of non-Noetherian S-rings. Moreover, in conjunction with existing works [19-23], our approach enables generalizations of well-known classical results, namely, Samelson's theorem, the Krein van der Waerden theorem, and the Carrasco-Moradi-Roldan theorem. A widely employed modulation technique, Gray-Coded encoding, is used in communication systems and is well-researched. A new approach called LLQ offers a computational solution by mapping binary sequences to low-bit representation using weight matrices. These enable us to categorize 3-APLs (3-vertex upward links) and demonstrate their relationship with a simplified crossing number concept. Additionally, we establish a new category, 2-SLs (2-vertex upward structures), and develop a crossing expression for 2-SLs, paralleling the single-layer aspect of Guennebaud and Lgarret's definition. Furthermore, we define a new graph model, X-bundles, to investigate both X-bundle crossings and upward compressibility in upplanarity. Finally, we examine the upplanarity complexity of a new family of graphs, Gkn for n ≥ 5. Despite being upplanarity-incomparable to previously studied graph families, the Gkn family challenges current upplanarity bounds and tests the efficiency of asymptotic upplanarity algorithms. A key objective is to upplanarize Gkn for the smallest possible n that allows division-free representations. For n ≤ 19, we demonstrate that such a division-free representation exists; in contrast, for n ≥ 20, we show that X-bundle crossings and division-based representations are essential for upplanarity. Human-based crowdsourcing in visual recognition tasks has the potential to rapidly gather ground truth labels for thousands of images. Nonetheless, the quality of the collected data is ultimately a reflection of how well individuals perform, as illustrated by variations in the output distributions known as 'human softmax' for the same image across multiple annotators. This study introduces an approach to leverage this information to quantify how reliable each annotation is. The method involves combining class probabilities from noisy data with an accurate model, and it uses a measure of entropy to find the optimal balance between the two. The idea is based on the concept that more reliable annotators provide more useful information, and as a result, the model can learn more when working with less noisy data from those experts. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves consistent performance regardless of the level of annotation noise, and it outperforms traditional techniques in cases with moderate noise levels of up to 20%. Additionally, the study showcases the practical application of this method, as it is used in a real-world crowdsourcing project to evaluate the reliability of annotations provided by human annotators. The approach is known as Crowd Sort. 

In this research, I have delved into several related topics, starting with modeling techniques for noisy data. Specifically, I have explored how combining a reliable model and noisy data from different sources can improve the accuracy of the model. Moreover, I have examined the concept of using ground truth distributions known as 'human softmax' to assess the reliability of each annotation. Finally, I have applied this method to a real-world project, effectively evaluating the accuracy of each annotator and using their performance to identify the top contributors for inference. 

Ensemble modeling was particularly investigated for its potential to leverage diverse sources of noisy data, and the application of information theory to create a metric of uncertainty that helps identify the most reliable annotations. 

Lastly, I have delved into active learning as a means of utilizing the method to prioritize and select annotations from less reliable individuals to provide more precise labels.

Question answering (QA) is an important task in which the goal is to determine if a given question has been answered truly or false based on provided information in a database. However, a critical challenge in implementing a fully automated QA system is dealing with the impact of ambiguous word meanings, which complicate the process of determining document relevance and require a deeper analysis of sentence context to resolve these ambiguies. To address this issue, our proposed method involves using a combination of natural language processing techniques to create a set of modified questions that are tailored to specific senses of ambiguous words, with the aim of identifying a relevant sentence that provides the correct answer to the original query. Importantly, this approach does not make any assumptions about the structure of the ambiguous word's dictionary or its multiple senses, which are typically required in prior methodologies. Instead, our system uses crowd-sourced data that contains examples of words paired with their associated meanings to enable it to operate effectively in a real-world setting. To test its effectiveness, we developed a method for integrating this word-sense disambiguation approach into a state-of-the-art real-world QA system, with the result being substantial gains in its performance on a database consisting of movie information. Specifically, our system was demonstrated to achieve an improvement of more than 15 percentage points in its accuracy rate for answering movie-related questions that feature contextually ambiguous words. We found that by employing this approach, it is possible to address the issue of ambiguous word meanings in natural language context without requiring any form of dictionary lookup or specialized knowledge retrieval infrastructure. All of the accompanying material, including source code and crowd-sourced data, is available for download on our public GitHub repository. The study of an individual's speaking style as a indicator of their mental condition has a long history, dating back to 1890 when a psychologist developed a method to analyze speech patterns. Building on this idea, researchers in this field now use advanced technologies such as computer-assisted techniques to analyze large datasets and identify reliable indicators of speech style. By achieving success in detecting depression from speech patterns, they are now working to create a comprehensive system for monitoring mental health through speech analysis. This research takes a significant step towards an entirely new method for analyzing speech to assess mental health by defining a particular phenomenon called entrainment. A new measure called entrainment distance measures how similar an individual's speech style is to the surrounding conversation. We trained a deep neural network to calculate this measure from raw audio, making it possible to analyze entrainment in spoken dialogue without manual transcription. We tested its accuracy on data with fully transcribed conversations and found that it performs well compared to the existing method for analyzing entrainment. Although it achieves good results on the standard corpus, we discovered that it works less effectively on a more challenging dataset for conversational dialogue. We hope that our work on entrainment will lead to new findings and further develop the ability to analyze audio from dialogue. We release our code and data for other researchers to use. Ultimately, while we believe that our method for analyzing entrainment is an important step towards an automated system for monitoring mental health through speech analysis, we recognize that mental health is a complex topic requiring thorough expertise and research. We plan to continue working to make our system more robust and reliable in the future. Until then, we are committed to explaining our system as a demonstration of advances in natural language processing technology. The explanation of our system is based on the understanding that entrainment is a universal aspect of human interaction - people naturally adapt their speech style to the context and tend to repeat patterns of sound and meaning. By analyzing this pattern, we can gain insight into an individual's thought processes. We are working to develop a system for analyzing entrainment that is useful, not just for researchers. While we are making significant progress in this area, we are also aware that much work remains to be done. We hope that our contributions will lead to new breakthroughs in this field and that our system will one day be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners across many areas. The potential applications of this system are vast and varied. The future of this system is what we hope to develop and expand upon going forward. We have developed an open-source platform called RCSED, a suite of browser-based tools for creating interactive visualizations of astronomical images and spectra. With RCSED, users can leverage high-level programming languages like Python and Type-Script to customize their web-based visualizations without requiring knowledge of web programming. RCSED enables users to create complex image and spectral profiles using Python functions and display them dynamically, along with showcasing reduced 1D and 2D spectra and their associated errors. Reduced spectra can be animated to illustrate variations over time. In addition, RCSED includes features to accurately draw contours from 2D spectra and calculate noise levels in individual apertures. We have also created a new slice simulator tool that allows users to generate artificial spectra and images from observed data, and we have released the platform as rcsed.org, accompanied by a comprehensive GitHub repository hosting the source code and demonstrating its numerous applications. As an example of RCSED's capabilities, we present a new tool for automatically identifying individual emission lines. Users can access the platform directly at rcsed.org, and the source code is available on GitHub at github.com/rcsed/rcsed-frontend and github.com/rcsed/rcsed-backend. Furthermore, we have developed a new tool for generating artificial spectra and images based on real data, which is available at specsimulator.org. Most existing research on action detection is focused on controlled, human-labeled data, making it difficult to apply in real-world scenarios. This work addresses the task of unsupervised action detection from raw video. It introduces a new method called SSCAP, a self-supervised parser that uses co-occurring class information to improve performance. SSAP, a previously studied parser, is enhanced by replacing its hand-coded class-bias statistics with learned weights derived from non-parametric density estimation. SSCAP achieves better results on the raw data by effectively learning relevant class information through self-supervision and subsequent fine-tuning with weak labelling, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods on unsupervised action detection. We also introduce a new evaluation protocol for evaluating weakly-labeled unsupervised action detection methods. Experiments on THUMOS-48 show that SSCAP surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The code for SSCAP can be found at \url{https://github.com/tony1120/SSCAP}.  In addition, our work on unsupervised action detection is distinct from that of flow-guided video parsing in the semantic segmentation of pre-trained models and neighboring action recognition tasks. Utilizing the light-cone QCD sum rules, we explore the general algebraic pattern of hidden-charm pentaquark states, starting from their formation and addressing critical issues in their analysis. Prolonging the sum rules to a high spectral density region, we examine the spontaneous breakdown of chiral symmetry in the pentaquark's Yukawa coupling. Moreover, we delve into the algebraic connections between the pentaquark and di-jetty states, resolving the long-standing mystery in their transition dynamics, and outlining the process of their decomposition. This research marks a significant milestone in understanding the pentaquark's internal composition and their journey from creation to dissolution. Student involvement in software testing courses can be challenging due to the subject matter's unique characteristics, which this paper aims to address by exploring the benefits of an inquiry-based learning approach versus a traditional feedback system. By incorporating QR codes or similar technology in a testing-related task, instructors can provide students with detailed feedback while also gauging their understanding of specific broader technological concepts, namely Agile, DevOps, IoT, Cyber Security, and Cloud Computing. A study comparing the outcomes of two sections of a testing course – one receiving conventional feedback and the other receiving inquiry-based learning feedback – led to a pilot examination involving 164 students. Domain adjustment, the task of adapting a model to a target domain without target data, is an essential problem when model predictions need to be consistent across different domains. However, standard domain adjustment techniques that use source and target data are not feasible in real-world scenarios, as they require access to target data. Existing solutions to this problem, known as source-free domain adjustment, rely on a model pre-trained on similar sources without using target data. Unfortunately, these solutions often fail when the source and target domains differ significantly. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that combines a source model with target domain information, known as pseudo-adjustment. By providing the adjustment information without requiring target data, our method overcomes a major issue in source-free domain adjustment. Additionally, we develop a technique to obtain multiple source models, each pre-trained on different datasets, to improve the robustness of our approach. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our novel approach in adjusting for significant domain shifts, outperforming existing source-free domain adjustment techniques. In a GCR system, a nuclear reaction occurs within a gas core contained by an inner container, generating heat that produces propellant gas in the system's fuel, typically 4He, and produces propellant gas in the system's exhaust, typically hydrogen. In a rocket ship, this propellant gas is used for propulsion. In a cycle where energy is retained, a nuclear reaction occurs in the gas core, and it's then transferred to a heat exchanger where it exchanges heat with a working fluid. This heated fluid is then expelled from the system's fuel, and it's then transferred to a turbine to generate electricity, which it does by exchanging heat with the 4He in the gas core. This process is repeated to maintain the nuclear reaction. In a cycle where energy is not retained, the GCR is air-cooled, and it's not part of the system's fuel. In an energy-retained cycle, the GCR is insulated and is not losing heat, and in an energy-non-retained cycle, the GCR is losing heat. The GCR gaseous fuel's high atomic number and energy output make it an ideal option for deep space propulsion, and it's able to achieve a high specific impulse. To address this gap, we have expanded the exoplanet-habitability information and precision spectroscopy database (EXOPLINES) to include absorption cross-sections for atmospheres of giant exoplanets and brown dwarfs, supplemented by a user-friendly online tool for computing spectral flux distributions and opacity maps. To maintain the highest level of versatility, we have provided the option to select various simplification levels for the data, ranging from complete molecular lists to synthetic curvatures for spectral lines. With the inclusion of EXOPLINES, we have responded to the growing demand for accessible, diverse, and extensive spectroscopic data for various celestial bodies. To facilitate data interpretation for various observation scenarios and astronomical objects, we have also provided a useful data visualizer. To model the thermal equilibrium of planetary and brown dwarf atmospheres, we have used two methods: the $T_{\rm eff}$-exponential model and the $p$-exponential model. We have compared these approaches to high-resolution observations of several objects across multiple wavelengths, with the $T_{\rm eff}$-exponential model proving effective in describing observations in the near-infrared and ultraviolet spectrums of Janssen, HD189733, HD209458, and KELT-9b. Conversely, the $p$-exponential model successfully simulated planetary phase curves of Hot Jupiters for various wavelengths by accounting for second-order effects, with the most notable applications being in models of Super-Earths, Venus, and exoplanet atmospheres. We have provided and made available for download precomputed spectral flux and opacity maps for various celestial bodies in EXOPLINES. These datasets include spectra of HD189733b, Jupiter, Jupiter's Great Red Spot, KELT-9b, Super Earth models, Venus, and several benchmark brown dwarfs. This disturbance was triggered by a powerful coronal mass ejection that formed an overpressured region at the equatorial low corona, linked to a bright radio burst.  To analyze this event precisely, researchers used a 3D wave equation model along with observations of the event's direction and scale.  It was found that the shock wave had a speed of approximately 185 km/s, and the pressure causing the overpressured region had a scale of about 0.35 solar radii.  By comparing the observed depression in brightness and the 171 Å photospheric brightening, the pressure causing the overpressured region was found to be around 2.4 dyn/cm$^2$ above atmospheric pressure at the equator. We introduce a monitored learning protocol, where the algorithm receives meta-data alongside the time series, as seen in protein sequences where occurrences of specific patterns (e.g. 'P' followed by 'O' then 'L') indicate a particular functional site (e.g. proline sites) while the rest is considered noise. This approach, tested using artificial data as well as real Drosophila genomics, successfully identifies relevant patterns within noisy, multi-variable data when given relevant meta-data. This monitored learning protocol is made accessible through the CorrelatedTimeSeries R package, which provides an R-based implementation. Reinforcement learning strategies, such as recurrent designs, are often used to tackle complex tasks involving hidden characteristics or delayed outcomes, which can be modeled as partially observable environments. Real-world tasks like managing uncertainty in financial forecasting or processing speech signals in signal processing can be effectively addressed through the use of recurrent architectures, which are able to capture and utilize hidden information or focus on critical outcomes. Interestingly, this expertise can also apply to analyzing human decision-making processes, specifically convictions in jury trials, where various factors like tendentious reasoning may influence the final outcome. From a machine learning perspective, this raises the question of whether algorithmic biases, whether hidden or apparent, can impact decision-making tasks, and if so, how a neutral system can be designed to minimize such biases and enhance fairness. Our work focuses on the intersection of cognitive science and the social sciences, using a convolutional neural network model to distinguish between the primary argument presented in a given speech file and the additional supporting arguments provided by the jury. This model is then used to evaluate the influence of hidden information, specifically the primary argument, on the final outcome of a verdict. Ultimately, our findings are particularly relevant in the context of jurisdictions that rely on oral presentations during trials. Our research is being made available as open-source at our repository, and readers are encouraged to access the associated blog post for further information. A future publication will provide an in-depth analysis of the underlying code, its implementation, and its potential applications. Our work is the first to analyze the connection between hidden information, regardless of its origin or nature, and its impact on decision-making processes using a machine learning approach. Consequently, this research opens up new avenues for exploring the relationship between hidden mental states and real-world application scenarios, which could potentially shed more light on the differences between human and machine decision-making processes. Moreover, this study is part of a broader series of projects aimed at leveraging AI-powered reinforcement learning, so readers are encouraged to visit the corresponding GitHub repository for further information. Current action detection methods heavily depend on strong and costly supervision to locate relevant video segments containing specific actions. This requirement leads to a labor-intensive annotation process due to the need for multiple boundary annotations per each class, per each video. Our proposed framework addresses this issue by training a neural network to identify key video frames based on limited class labels, allowing it to identify action-related frames across various videos, regardless of class-specific annotations. This framework then employs a graph convolutional network to capture context, represented by the interactions between key frames, which enhances performance compared to only focusing on individual key frames. Our experiments show that with minimal guidance – class names and no boundary annotations – our system achieves state-of-the-art action detection results on HMDB51, UCF51, and the Kinetics Human Action dataset. Additionally, our framework significantly outperforms the current best approach on the larger, heavily-kinship-related Kinship dataset. This study is the first to apply graph convolutional networks to action detection, improving performance by learning context, particularly in complex scenarios and difficult actions. Importantly, our framework reduces guidance requirements, making it a scalable and efficient solution. Code is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/swegc. Previous studies have suggested that neural network-based artificial intelligence
systems tend to favor similarity over novelty, a trend known as "overfitting to
visual patterns". To investigate this phenomenon further, a two-part challenge
was held - the Image Resemblance Challenge - consisting of a competition to
identify images that resembled each other and a separate competition to
discover new and distinct image categories. Participants in the challenge used
a diverse array of AI models and data sets, including images of human faces,
buddhas from an unlabelled collection, and a comprehensive data set featuring
a wide range of objects. Analysis of the results revealed that nearly all the
entered models, which included optimised models as well as less refined versions,
correctly identified similar images when the characteristics of the test set and
training data aligned. However, models struggled when the test set differed from
the training data. Moreover, it was found that models could learn to identify
distinct categories within images, such as different species of animals or
various types of objects, provided that novel categories were relatively few
in number. Surprisingly, models performed better on these tasks when using a
training approach involving contrastive learning. This approach involves comparing
multiple images with each other, identifying shared features and removing
distinguishable attributes. A new tool was also developed to automatically
determine whether networks overfit to visual patterns by identifying areas of
high similarity. This method was found to work as well for less refined models as
it did for those that were highly optimised. Importantly, it was found that
artificial intelligence systems that overfit to visual patterns are still very
effective at a range of tasks. A major limitation of the study was that the new
tool was tested using data sets featuring visual characteristics that change
gradually rather than abrupt ones and with relatively high similarity ranges
rather than low ones. Investigating these findings further using a broader
range of data sets would be beneficial. The full source code, data sets, documentation
and results are available at publicly shared locations. The Image Resemblance

The widely-accepted method of Resource Sharing in online educational settings relies on exchanging data between disparate parties. To address concerns about the privacy of sensitive educational data, researchers have recently introduced Differential Privacy techniques. Although previous approaches provided a basic level of privacy, they failed to account for the statistical relationships within the data, ultimately sacrificing usefulness for a modest level of privacy. Resource Sharing in educational settings demands either higher privacy or a more efficient method of information exchange. 

We present a novel approach to enhancing privacy through the statistical examination of two key factors: the mean and variance of student grades. Our model, DP-REC, uses the Hypergeometric Distribution to create a method of Information-Theoretic Differential Privacy for educational settings. DP-REC offers a level of privacy comparable to existing methods, but does so with improved usefulness. DP-REC is shown to be the most effective among recent approaches to Resource Sharing. We also present a method for determining the optimal balance between privacy and usefulness, an essential component for any method of Information-Theoretic Differential Privacy. Ultimately, our model, DP-REC, offers a level of privacy and usefulness superior to the widely-accepted approach of exchanging synthetic data. We compare DP-REC to synthetic data exchange in the context of three distinct educational tasks. Our model and the proposed approach of exchanging synthetic data are complementary solutions, providing a framework for the private and efficient exchange of educational information. 

A technical demonstration of DP-REC is available at this link: https://sites.google.com/view/dp-rcvii. The source code for DP-REC is available at this link: https://github.com/leothari/Differential-Privacy-Resource-Sharing. 

The results of our paper indicate that recent approaches to Resource Sharing in educational settings are outperformed by previous methods. We conclude that recent claims of recent approaches to Resource Sharing, boasting improved utility and privacy, are inaccurately represented in the literature. We provide a detailed analysis of the source code for DP-REC, as well as the code for discrete DP, recently introduced in the literature. 

A proposed modification to the framework for the Recourse Sharing Challenge is intended to enhance the accuracy and utility of educational information exchange in future challenges. We believe that recent approaches to Resource Sharing are underwhelming due to a lack of privacy or usefulness in the proposed framework. We intend to establish a new set of challenges for the Recourse Sharing Challenge, centered around the optimal balance of privacy and usefulness, as well as a method of information-theoretic differential privacy in educational information

We analyze complex, multi-step game scenarios in which players lack complete knowledge of payoff matrices. Our focus is on two-part games where players simultaneously determine and resolve commitments. We recognize that real-world decision-making often involves such situations, including negotiations, negotiations with biases, fair division of resources, and more. To tackle these incomplete information-based game scenarios, we explore two novel approaches. The first approach is an iterative learning system combined with a specific player strategy, which we call "Categorizing and Learning" (CAL). The second approach is an innovative adaptation of the concept of Nash Equilibrium (AE). Both methods are evaluated for their effectiveness in one-and two-player games, as well as for their broader theoretical implications. The results show that under specific conditions, these methods can guarantee stable outcomes similar to Nash Equilibria. Furthermore, we found that in situations where no Nash Equilibrium exists, the CAL approach is as effective as the most advanced fully-fitting decision theory. Interestingly, we observed that the CAL approach performs better when applied to situations of incomplete information compared to similar adaptive learning techniques in complete information-based game scenarios. Moreover, we observed a degree of similarity between the CAL approach and human decision-making and learning processes, which we discuss at length. The results suggest that an artificial intelligence system equipped with the CAL approach outperforms other decision-making methods in various applications. The typical approach for achieving this is by employing an overcomplete system of filters, where each filter represents a different possible query classification. However, since the total number of possible query classifications is often substantial, this method often results in a significant proportion of unnecessary, false-positive classifications. To address this limitation, we propose the introduction of a novel data structure called an APQC-list. APQC-list is a compact, probabilistic data structure specifically designed to perform approximate membership inquiries efficiently with no false positives. Our proposed filter has several desirable properties including efficient construction, allowing a false-positive-free collection to be represented using the same number of filters as the total number of possible query classifications. Our APQC-list, for example, reduces the storage requirement by 10% for the top 10,000 categories used by Google's FastFilter system to classify web pages, resulting in a more compact and efficient filter of 2.93 GB compared to 3.23 GB. Additionally, our APQC-list demonstrates approximately 2.7 times faster construction speed than FastFilter. A recently developed TTS model called FastPitch is capable of producing high-quality speech in both 16 kHz and 48 kHz formats. However, the model's speech quality is found to degrade slightly when significantly altered in pitch. To resolve this issue, researchers have proposed a pitch augmentation method called timbre preserve PitchFast that substantially improves pitch's manageability in FastPitch. To implement this method, two key changes were made to the model: 1) a decoupled frame setup was implemented which allows pitch adjustments to be determined independently for each frame; and 2) a residual term was added to enable the retrieval of original pitches. Experimental results demonstrate that PitchFast can recover pitches with high accuracy and significantly enhance the pitch adjustment capability of FastPitch. Moreover, the model can perform multi-step pitch adjustments as well as other complex pitch manipulation tasks such as pitch gliding. We explore a class of combinatorial games, referred to as token-firing games, which are played on the edges of a multigraph. Each edge corresponds to a mathematical function defined by its slope and y-intercept, and specific local rules govern when and how edges fire. A key concept related to game configurations involves the combination of cyclically ordered Jacobians and Prym varieties. By introducing a natural invariant on this product, we are led to investigate additional game constructions, including halting strategies and combinations, which are in turn related to the invariants of individual games. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which certain factorization properties for $A$-types and Tanner codes emerge. Along the way, we develop results on the relationship between certain configurations of token-firing games and numerical semigroups, as well as the geometry of halting curves. Additionally, we provide a detailed explanation of how token-firing games give rise to halting strategies for hyperelliptic Jacobians, generalizing existing results in the genus 2 case. As an outgrowth of this investigation, we describe a method for using token-firing games to construct curves with predetermined properties, which may be of independent interest. Finally, in the supplementary material for this article, we explore additional game constructions, including multigraphs with specified properties, halting strategies with extra structure, and combinations of games involving multiple edges. A few examples are provided to illustrate these generalizations. Furthermore, some challenging questions related to graph theory and curve arithmetic are proposed in the conclusion. Recent research indicates that deep neural networks often generalize better for similar tasks, a phenomenon known as transferability. However, the extent to which networks adapted to different datasets can accurately classify new data remains unclear. In this report, we reassess two commonly accepted assumptions about this phenomenon: firstly, that a well-adapted network is inherently more accurate, and secondly, that task similarity is the main determinant of transferability. Through our analysis, we demonstrate these two assumptions are false. Instead, we reveal that shared network complexities between datasets are a more significant indicator of transferability. Furthermore, we observe that task similarity plays a minor role. Additionally, we find that networks trained for longer periods tend to be less transferable. These findings, with supporting numerical examples, stress the importance of constraining model diversity when developing a network from another's weights for the same task, a task known as knowledge distillation. This highlights a major challenge in current distillation methods: though they achieve good in-dataset performance, their inability to achieve good out-of-dataset performance (i.e. with unseen data) is a major shortcoming. Conversely, the actual structure of the network, particularly characteristics such as its clustering coefficient and community number, have minimal to no impact on this propagation speed. Nevertheless, this research finds that by examining specific microscopic processes, a relationship can be established where the speed of information dissemination is positively correlated with the network's modular nature. Furthermore, an experimental study reveals a negative correlation between a community's density and the speed at which information is transmitted, particularly when employing a model using simultaneous multiple information carriers. An additional experiment discovered a positive connection between the number of a network's modules and the dissemination speed when using a model featuring sequential information carriers. These findings highlight the significance of network structure in understanding and predicting the speed at which information is transmitted. They also suggest two key governance factors: community density and community number, which can respectively hinder and promote information propagation. These results are particularly relevant in various real-world scenarios including the spread of contagions, financial information dissemination and communication processes occurring within the human brain. We introduce a quantitative form of the Thomas-Yau uniqueness conjecture, which states that for two Lagrangian fibration equivalent Hamiltonians, their Lagrangian embeddings will not intersect for positive time. We prove this new form for Hamiltonians with simple singularities and use this result to show the uniqueness of certain isotopies between Lagrangian fibration images. This leads to the classification of some local properties of fibration, particularly the uniqueness of monodromy groups, and a proof that equivalent fibration images have isotopic torus fibers. Furthermore, we extend the Yudin conjecture, which pertains to the distortion of Lagrangians, by proving the existence of Lagrangians with infinite distortion under certain conditions. We introduce new invariants based on the Alexander polynomial and prove these invariants are unique to each fibration class. We also derive compact versions of these invariants and show that equivalent fibration images must share these invariant properties. Finally, we prove that for fibration with a product monodromy, the Alexander polynomial invariants vanish and demonstrate this on known examples of monodromy groups, which includes torus fibers and those with a product monodromy. We explore the relationship between these results and the notched torus construction. Our methods involve proving the existence of Lagrangian tori with a specified intersection matrix and parallelism properties for any fibration. We prove the existence of these tori for any intersection matrix using Floer theory and multivariate cocycle perturbations, which has independent value. We derive compact versions of these tori using Floer theory and prove these tori are distinct for any fibration. Based on the results regarding the uniqueness of isotopies and the Thomas-Yau conjecture, we prove that for fibration with product monodromy, the notched torus construction is the only known example of Lagrangian tori with a specified intersection matrix. This leads to the conclusion that for fibration with product monodromy, the Alexander polynomial invariants are the most general known invariant properties of Lagrangians. We prove that for fibration, the Alexander polynomial invariants are unique to each translation of each fibration class. This leads to the conclusion that for fibration, the Alexander polynomial invariants are the most general known unique invariant properties of Lagrangians. The classical continuous-time Standard Perturbation Model for unamplified connections is a widely used method for assessing modulation error ratios and characterizing signal degradation caused by time delays in communication systems. This model relies on a power spectral density formula that leverages the Fourier transform of the system impulse response. To evaluate the accuracy of this model in discrete-time settings, a different approach is employed, where the delay is represented as a power spectral density in discrete form. We investigate discrete-time standards for M-QAM modulation methods in this context, focusing on M-QAM values from 4 to 2048. The analysis reveals negligible differences between continuous and discrete models for small M values, decreasing as M grows larger. Moreover, our findings suggest that the discrete model can serve as a precise approximation for M values exceeding 128. We further explore potential discrete-time standards and establish criteria for identifying valid discrete-time power spectral density representations of time-domain delay effects in discrete-time settings. Finally, our research demonstrates the validity of the discrete-time Standard Perturbation Model for M-QAM values from 4 to 2048, fulfilling the established criteria. We validate this model using M-QAM modulation methods with time delays up to 10% of the symbol period. As demonstrated through our M-QAM noise-perturbation simulation, the discrete-time Standard Perturbation Model offers high accuracy in estimating modulation error ratios, achieving ratios close to 100 percent for M values from 128 to 2048. We also show that the discrete-time Standard Perturbation Model is versatile, applicable to both single and multiple delayed unamplified connections. To facilitate potential use in M-QAM modulation methods with time delays, our discrete-time Standard Perturbation Model is a reliable tool for accurately modeling and simulating discrete-time power spectral density representations of time-domain delay effects in communication systems. We believe that the findings presented here can enhance precision in communication system modeling and testing. We provide discrete-time power spectral density formulas for M-QAM values from 4 to 2048, along with corresponding delay-spreading functions and discrete delay values. We offer our analysis and research in hopes that the findings presented here can contribute to advancements in modern communication system design. The numerical results and analysis discussed in this research solution are documented in a complementary Excel spreadsheet located at the end of this paper. We believe that the methods and data obtained from this research solution can be applied and extended further in the future. As the number of mobile devices increases, so does the value of user data, making it a target for malicious attacks. One type of attack that threatens mobile security is Insider Collusion Attack. Unlike traditional insider attacks, which focus on stealing data or installing spyware, insider collusion attacks involve combining legitimate services to create malicious functions. This is a unique set of challenges because the underlying issue lies in the service itself, not in how the services are used. In this context, we will be focusing on Issue-Space Evasion Assaults, which involve exploiting ambiguities in service specifications to enable malicious functionality. Our review of issue-space evasion assaults begins with an introduction to insider collusion attacks and their unique characteristics. Next, we provide a comprehensive overview of issue-space, focusing on what constitutes an issue and how issues are related to each other. We then delve into the evolution of issue-space evasion assaults, covering past and current attacks on Android. Finally, we outline future research directions inspired by issue-space evasion assaults and highlight potential risks if these threats are not adequately addressed. An implementation of our proposed research is available on GitHub under the name INSIDER. Issue-space evasion assaults represent a significant challenge for mobile security researchers because the underlying issue space is complex and multi-faceted. By hiding behind legitimate services, evasives have proven to be highly effective in bypassing detection. This makes issue-space evasion assaults a pressing concern that demands greater research attention and understanding. Given the significant potential losses users could face if these threats are not addressed effectively, it is essential that mobile security experts and researchers prioritize issue-space evasion assaults in their work. Our proposed research aims to fill the existing knowledge gap on issue-space evasion assaults through systematic and practical means. By contributing to this area of research, we aim to protect mobile users and advance mobile security more effectively. The primary contribution of our work involves identifying and exploring issue-space evasion assaults, which have received limited attention in past research. By conducting an in-depth analysis of the domain, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of issue-space evasion assaults that can inform and guide researchers and practitioners alike. The world of mobile security is highly dynamic, with new challenges and threats emerging every day. Given the significant potential losses users could face if these threats are not addressed effectively, it is essential that mobile security experts and researchers prioritize issue-space evasion assaults in their work. This research aims to protect mobile users and advance mobile security more effectively. The proposed framework is unique because it focuses on concrete, actionable advice that researchers and practitioners can use to address issue-space evasion assaults

Our findings indicate that solutions to pebble accretion often depend on the nature of these turbulent fluctuations. For example, in cases where the disk exhibits density fluctuations, a wide distribution of particles tends to facilitate giant planet formation. In contrast, when the disk's viscosity is the focus, particles are more likely to accumulate near the disk's surface, while wide distributions yield smaller, terrestrial planets that form closer to the star, increasing the likelihood of capturing orbit around the star. Overparameterization is a prominent feature of modern machine learning, particularly when combined with regularization. This tendency suggests that the underlying predictive model used by the algorithm may differ significantly from the target concept to be learned. However, empirical observations indicate that overparameterized models still achieve good performance and often outperform conservatively parameterized ones. Prior research offers some computational explanations for this phenomenon, but they are largely tied to issues of optimization efficiency, dataset size, and overfitting. This study explores another potential explanation, focusing on the algorithm's predictive task as a communication complexity problem. It demonstrates that in certain concept learning scenarios, overparameterization is necessary to overcome the algorithm's computational constraints. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the time complexity of interpolation algorithms is influenced by the algorithm's data-dependent difficulty of prediction. While this result does not consider generalization performance, it provides an explanation for the overparameterization trend when solely evaluating interpolation efficiency. Finally, experiments on real-world data support the idea that overparameterization is beneficial for convergence time, an aspect of prediction tasks. Overall, the research emphasizes the significance of viewing algorithms through both the perspective of concept learning and computational complexity. It also adds a new layer of understanding to the role of overparameterization in overparameterized models by focusing on the algorithm's predictive difficulty rather than its output coverage. As such, the research contributes to the growing body of work seeking to elucidate the implications of overparameterization. Moreover, the study explores novel prediction tasks to demonstrate that concept learning is a valuable perspective for analyzing algorithms, and the research ties the time complexity of interpolation algorithms to the time complexity of the underlying prediction task. Lastly, the study's findings on predictive data flow complexity provide fresh insights into the relationship between computation and data structure in predictive tasks. Such insights could potentially be extended to other models, including neural networks composed of artificial neurons. They could also inspire future investigations into the relationship between predictive tasks and data distribution, and how this relationship impacts the performance of time-complexity-based measures. The Dial-a-Ride Problem (DRP) is a challenging task in the field of vehicle scheduling, particularly when considering the optimal assignment of customers to vehicles and the routing of vehicles to minimize total travel costs. DRP is a highly complex problem, with large local optimizations that make it difficult to identify optimal solutions efficiently. In this paper, we propose a new approach to tackle the dial-a-ride problem by branching on vehicle sets and using reduced complex demand for customers to simplify the routing process. We also introduce a bound estimation method, based on an approximation of the routing optimality, and provide a method to estimate a lower bound for the solution. We tested our algorithm on 24 instances of the DRP, with 7 vehicles and up to 10 customers, and obtained optimal results for all the tested cases. The algorithm's efficiency is further illustrated by a set of experimental results which show a significant improvement in solution time as a result of bounding the vehicle sets. The analysis of the obtained results highlights the importance of considering both vehicle and routing optimality to identify optimal solutions efficiently. The proposed algorithm, with its reduced complex demand, shows promising potential to be used as a starting point for heuristic approaches aiming to improve vehicle scheduling and routing practices in metropolitan areas. The research findings provide valuable insights for improving vehicle scheduling and routing in urban settings. The evaluations conducted on multiple E-commerce datasets demonstrate that IRIS significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy. The research on Alzheimer's disease is particularly challenging due to its gradual progression, often going undetected until late stages when effective treatment becomes difficult. A key aspect of managing the disease is precise diagnosis, which relies on distinguishing between healthy individuals, individuals with mild cognitive symptoms, and those with full-blown Alzheimer's. This study focuses on using magnetic resonance imaging data of brain structures to identify three diagnostic stages of Alzheimer's: normal cognitive function, mild cognitive impairment, and severe Alzheimer's disease. The researchers employed the Deep InfoMax method to create features from MRI data, which were combined with traditional imaging features for a comprehensive analysis. A support vector machine was used for classification, initially evaluating the relevance of each feature type, then re-examining the task with the full set of features. A key contribution of this study lies in exploring the potential for deep learning to improve the diagnosis and progression forecasting of Alzheimer's disease. Notably, the study's findings suggest that feature extraction with Deep InfoMax enhances the performance of an SVM classifier when compared to a baseline model. Moreover, the study's proposed method outperformed other competition results in forecasting the progression of Alzheimer's disease stages. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative as part of a organized competition to advance the diagnosis and forecasting of distinct stages in Alzheimer's progression. The study's code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/leotieul/DeepInfoMax_ADI. The research was executed on a graphics processing unit computing platform. The study's outcomes reveal that feature extraction with Deep InfoMax, combined with an SVM classifier, achieves accurate results for diagnosing cognitive impairment and forecasting the progression of Alzheimer's disease stages, even with a limited set of structural brain structure features. These methods were competitive in the 2015 Image Retrieval/Alzheimer's Disease (IR/AD) competition. A key finding shows that MRI data of posterior brain structures significantly contributes to accurate diagnosis and forecasting, outperforming other competition results. This research provides a method for using deep learning to improve structural brain structure feature extraction from MRI scans and supporting an accurate diagnostic tool and forecasting model for distinct stages in Alzheimer's progression. The study's conclusions highlight the importance of using deep learning to improve diagnostic accuracy and forecasting capabilities in neurodeenerative diseases. As AI modeling advances, there is an increasing demand for systems that can withstand significant and unexpected shifts in data distribution.  In the realm of AI-assisted healthcare,  testing on real-world data, rather than simulated environments,  is crucial in assessing tools used for clinical trial design.  One significant limitation in utilizing conventional machine learning models is their inability to accurately predict performance outside of their training domain.  A key challenge in clinical trials is predicting exam performance in patients who have not undergone an exam, given exam-positive and exam-negative data.  A proposed solution is an empirical forecasting model called conformal prediction.  A specific type of conformal predictive interval, known as the.632+ conformal interval, offers several desirable properties,  including high confidence in its coverage and robustness to data manipulation.  In this study,  we apply the.632+ method to the prediction of exam performance in AI-assisted healthcare instruments.  An AI system was used to simulate real-world data on patients who either had or did not have an exam,  and was then trained and tested in successive iterations,  with the exception of one,  in order to analyze its predicted performance in exam-positive scenarios.  The proposed approach successfully estimated correct exam-positive rates in 8 out of 10 instances.  An additional 10 testing period confirmed that the predicted exam-positive rate varied between 0.25 and 0.35.  The predicted accuracy of the model itself also underwent significant improvement,  rising from 0.66 to 0.88.  The proposed approach's predicted exam-positive rate was found to be 0.16,  which compares favorably to a baseline of 0.1 established by expert review.  The proposed architecture's complexity was shown to be comparable to that of a linear model.  An upcoming study will investigate the generalizability of the proposed approach to other distribution shift situations.  The proposed code is openly available on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/andreaborelli/conformal-prediction.  Future work will focus on the study's generalizability to other predictive distribution shift situations.  The proposed code is openly available.  The proposed study's findings suggest that the.632+ method can accurately predict exam-positive rates in AI healthcare instruments under realistic domain shift conditions.  An upcoming study will investigate the study's external validity.  The proposed code is openly available.  The proposed study's findings suggest that the.632+ method has potential in AI healthcare.

The findings show that the platform helps to remove unwanted minima in the energy landscape, allowing for faster exploration of the DNA's configuration space. Additionally, we used the platform to simulate longer DNA segments and a tetraplex DNA structure, which require an even more significant bias. It can be incorporated into existing simulation tools at little additional computational cost. With this approach, researchers may achieve substantial improvements in the correlation between simulation and experimental data. Future motion predictions in crowded environments significantly benefit from considering the intentions and future behaviors of all individuals involved. Most current methods focus solely on the immediate past activities of people within a confined context, overlooking important social aspects and neglecting the interconnectedness of people's movements over time. This paper presents a novel approach that comprehends people's past and future interactions through the integration of two advanced predictive models. Firstly, a Sliding CVAE model generates sequential predictions by gradually building upon previous forecasts, ensuring consistency in the state estimation. Secondly, a socially-aware model reexamines these predictions from multiple future perspectives, identifying potential individuals' goals, and thus refines the overall forecast trajectory. We evaluate our proposed approach against state-of-the-art models on two complex datasets, demonstrating its superior performance in predicting human motion in crowded settings. You can find more information and implementation details at https://github.com/andreabicchi/S2CVAE. Experimental results show that our method consistently outperforms baseline models, providing accurate and socially-aware predictions in crowded environments. Notably, our approach surpasses baseline models by at least 35% in terms of ADE and FDE on the Real29 dataset. On the Stanford2D3D dataset, our method achieves significant improvements, with performance enhancements of 27% in terms of ADE and 32% in terms of FDE. Moreover, our method appears to be more resistant to model memorization, as evidenced by the analysis conducted on the Stanford2D3D dataset. The average ADE and FDE obtained by our method are 12.64 and 18.35 respectively. These results suggest that our approach effectively predicts human motion in crowded settings by modeling sequential and socially-aware transitions between states. The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving lower error rates of at least 27% in terms of ADE and at least 32% in terms of FDE on the Stanford2D3D dataset. Although the generalization capability of our method was not directly evaluated, its performance on the Real29 dataset reveals a moderate sensitivity to data properties, with a 10% increase in error rate observed for every decade of age gap between the training and testing data. Therefore, it is essential to consider properties such as appearance and behavior similarity when collecting and labeling datasets to ensure that they effectively generalize across different cases. It investigates whether single measures can adequately capture a network's dynamic characteristics, including behavior and statistical information, or if a need exists for more nuanced approaches to capture a network's dynamic nature. Furthermore, it examines whether a certain class of measures is more suitable for certain information-theoretic tasks, such as evaluating a network's ability to transmit information through its connections. Empirical results indicate that a network's ability to transmit information generally aligns with other complexity measures, though exceptions exist. Consequently, a case can be made for using a diversity of complexity measures to capture a network's dynamic characteristics, rather than relying on a single measure, to obtain a more comprehensive understanding. Interestingly, the findings also suggest that a network's ability to transmit information is often adequately captured by simpler measures, such as its normalized entropy or degree of homogeneity. Nevertheless, the empirical analysis also reveals that a network's ability to transmit information can be negatively affected by factors such as network fragmentation, the structure of its community structures, and the connections existing between them, as evidenced by observations made across a variety of artificially generated networks. A novel technique, high-velocity decoloration (HVD), is able to erase color patterns in complex environments with high precision, making it ideal for industrial use where intricate 3D surfaces require pattern removal. Research in HVD has focused on understanding its fundamental behavior and improving accuracy in various applications. Although previous studies controlled HVD timing to optimize performance, an experimental investigation of the effects of slowing HVD on arbitrary surfaces had not been conducted until now. In this research, we observed the effects of decelerating HVD on how quickly a surface regains its natural color. We discovered that HVD can be divided into four distinct stages: rapid color removal, reaching the peak decoloration rate, temperature stabilization, and a color recovery phase that occurs at different rates for three types of surfaces - polymer and PMMA, brass, and skin-toned silicone. Since the melting points of these surfaces vary significantly, we propose using an approach that combines color information with temperature measurements, which is based on an established color model. When applied to HVD, this approach allows us to predict when and to what extent the surface will recover its original color based on the characteristics of the surfaces involved. An algorithm for calculating this color recovery is presented along with an associated timing curve that can be used for optimizing HVD timing. An alternative approach, tint mapping, is also explored, which allows for rapid application of a new color pattern on a variety of surfaces. An experimental tint curve is developed in conjunction with the proposed recovery algorithm. Both the recovery and tint curves can be used in models of HVD's complex interaction with surfaces, which may have applications in future research. A potential application of this research is in developing a method for automatically adjusting HVD timing for specific materials. Transformers' reliance on a single, exchangeable embedding space has led to a
need for regularization techniques to mitigate overfitting. A relatively new
approach involves using a separate "tangent space" for each head of the
multihead self-attention mechanism in the Transformer architecture. This study
presents an innovative approach where each head has its own unique tangent space
in an autoencoder setup, allowing the use of directionality constraints while
maintaining the flexibility to represent different head dimensions in separate
spaces. This method is named Non-Exchangeable Transformer-K (NFT-K) and is
demonstrated to be effective on the GLUE benchmark for natural language processing. Furthermore, NFT-K is applied in the field of natural language generation, showing promising results. An implementation of the NFT-K algorithm is available on GitHub at the specified repository. Experimental findings indicate that NFT-K is comparable to other non-exchangeable models in efficiency and effectiveness, outperforming the standard exchangeable embedding approach in efficiency and achieving substantial improvements in effectiveness. Moreover, NFT-K is found to be more robust to the hyperparameters of a language model it was integrated with. The end result is that NFT-K is a more attractive option compared to other multi-head attention approaches, leading to a new direction in the field of transformer architectures. Additionally, our work highlights the potential benefits of using tangent spaces in the field of sequence-to-sequence tasks in natural language processing and shows promising results for NFT-K in the task of sequence generation. NFT-K is also found to be the first method to successfully apply dimensionality reduction to the distribution of attention weights, leading to a new area of exploration. Our method is found to improve the state-of-the-art performance in the task of sequence generation by improving the BLEU score, with the NFT-K variant that uses Gaussian distribution for the last tangent space having a BLEU score of 11.96, which surpasses the previous best known result of 10.93. Moreover, our method is found to be highly applicable as it achieves significant improvements in multiple downstream tasks. The end result is that NFT-K is considered a powerful tool in the field of natural language processing. The code for NFT-K is available on GitHub at the repository provided at the end of this work. NFT-K achieved state-of-the-art performance in the task of text generation by improving the BLEU score when compared to previous models, providing new insights to the field of natural language processing. A category of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems, known as non-Hermitian Chern bands, has gained recent attention. They are characterized by exceptional states protected by a combination of non-Hermitian boundary conditions and time-reversal symmetry in a static, interacting framework. We provide a general theoretical framework to study these systems, using a effective low-energy Hamiltonian based on a nearest-neighbor model. Furthermore, we offer numerical guidelines to establish a neighboring point-gap topological phase in a theory of fermionic time-reversal symmetric systems. Additionally, we investigate how non-zero tunneling between branches of the band structure affects these systems. Our research shows that interactions and intra-band connections can reduce the topological protection of the system. Finally, we discuss recent experimental realizations of these systems, which have involved nonequilibrium dynamics and collinear magnetic ordering, respectively. We outline new directions for future research on this growing class of topological systems. Using density matrix renormalization group simulations of interacting fermions, our work highlights the protective role of time-reversal symmetry in a nearest-neighbor model. A new nearest-neighbor particle-hole symmetric model has been constructed which has a Z2 topological invariant similar to a Kramers pair of non-interacting Majorana edge modes. A ground-state degeneracy associated with time-reversal symmetry is present in the bulk when the model is in the gapped phase. Our simulations show that the wave function of the model for one of the ground states exhibits the properties of a non-Hermitian Chern band. Specifically, the wave function exhibits chiral behavior in its amplitudes at different points in space and we are able to measure the chiral magnetic effect in the boundary. Our results show that the model can be reduced to a nonequilibrium nearest-neighbor fermionic model by removing the long-range hopping term. A variant of the Haldane model has been constructed which eliminates the topological protection of the system when the model is in the gapped phase. A similar approach has been taken to destroy the topological protection of time-reversal symmetric Majorana edge modes in a model that models ferromagnetic ordering. Our research shows that the model for one of the ordering types remains topological while for the other the model is in the bulk of a midgap state. Finally, future research on this class of topological systems is outlined. Our research project aimed to develop characteristics that represent individual speakers through speaker traits and incorporate these into synthetic speech. We collected a diverse dataset of speaker characteristics from a substantial number of listeners and evaluated the accuracy of the obtained features using multiple evaluation methods. We also investigated how speaker characteristics and linguistic factors interact and influenced the perception of synthetic speech. We found that the perceived quality of speech generated using a standard TTS approach was improved when incorporating speaker characteristics, but the effect was reversed when considering the interaction between speaker characteristics and linguistic content. This interaction had a significant positive impact on the perceived quality of the speech. We demonstrated the importance of integrating speaker characteristics and interpreted the results through the lens of the speaker's social background. Further details on the study can be accessed at https://sopeark.github.io/sopeark-tacit. The data and code used in this study, as well as the TTS model fine-tuned in our research, can be accessed at https://sopeark.github.io/tacit-sopeark. The TTS model was trained without incorporating gender information, resulting in a uniform distribution of the TTS model's perceived quality across male and female identities. Our research was part of a broader examination of the TTS model's robustness to its output's social identity. The results of this study were presented at the Interspeech 2021 conference. Utilizing this approach, we obtain narrow width parameters for the three-dimensional collective potential energy. From the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian, we calculate energy levels and examine the properties of low-l states in triaxial nuclei, particularly in nuclei close to the gamma unstable axis. A key finding is that minimal distance occurs near the middle of three-dimensional collective potential energy. This method is validated through the analysis of experimental energy levels in low-l states of triaxial nuclei, which show good agreement with theoretical findings. A novel deep convolutional autoencoder (DCA) based method is proposed for detecting unknown alterations in hyperspectral images. By utilizing a combined feature of both the original image and the image with identified changes, and a learned low-dimensional representation of the altered areas, it is possible for the classifier to identify various types of anomalies. Experimental results obtained from two hyperspectral datasets reveal that the method effectively detects unknown alterations in images, outperforming other existing techniques such as the locally linear discriminant manifold-based detector and the deep learning based locally linear discriminant manifold-based detector. A detailed analysis is performed on the theoretical background of model potentials that replicate the behavior of nonpolar molecular fluids in their liquid and gas phases. To assess the performance of these potentials, comparisons are made between remaining entropies and viscosity values derived from simulations of (i) model potentials and (ii) actual molecular systems, both in their pure forms and when paired with nonpolar partners. When paired, the comparisons involve calculations of entropy reductions and ratios, and disentanglement factors. On the other side, the examination of ultrasonic velocities and viscosities in mixtures provides a separate assessment of model potentials. An original method for evaluating remaining entropies of pairs is also introduced, along with a key finding regarding the remaining entropy ratio: it appears: $\sigma_r^{AA}/\sigma_r^{BB} = \sigma_r^{AB}/\sigma_r^{BB} = 0.188 \; \epsilon/k_B$ for all model potentials considered. Consequently, a similar balance is found in molecular systems described by pair potential models near the critical area. Moreover, the remaining entropy of pairs is shown to be directly related to the degree of molecular association, as well as to entropy contributions from translational and rotational motion. An alternative approach to determining the disentanglement factor is presented, based on potential energy distribution along with radial distribution functions that describe contact between like and unlike molecules. Both high and low-temperature disentanglement factors were studied: the former corresponds to model potentials, the latter to experimental conditions. The study reveals a simple model for disentanglement factors that matches well with simulation results for all model potentials. Finally, observations are made about the impact of remaining entropy on the phase behavior of nonpolar mixtures, as well as the need to consider the role of potential energy in the relationship between entropy and viscosity. An example of this is the case of N2 + CO2, where it is observed that the remaining entropy of the mixture does not follow the ideal-mixture contribution, but rather matches the remaining entropy of the guest component when paired with argon. Consequently, it is proposed that the remaining-entropy contribution could be used to determine the disentanglement factor and thus provide valuable information on intermolecular forces in nonpolar mixtures. An illustration of this is the case of CH4 + CF4, where the disentanglement factor determined from remaining-entropy contributions agrees with those derived from experimental and simulation ultrasonic velocity measurements and molecular dynamics simulations, respectively. Existing solutions fall short in addressing this need, as they either fail to provide performance guarantees or compromise reliability. A new approach, using hypervisor technology, is presented, demonstrating the capability to enhance embedded real-time system security through fault isolation. Furthermore, hypervisor performance is typically manageable, making them a desirable option. Nevertheless, hypervisor development is complicated by the absence of suitable design architectures and efficient resource management mechanisms. 

This research introduces T-Visor, an open-source hypervisor, specifically designed to support mixed-importance embedded real-time systems through virtualization technology. T-Visor incorporates a novel CPU resource scheduling algorithm, called HWH_RSF, and an memory virtualization mechanism, called MVME, designed to improve performance and efficiency. A combined evaluation of T-Visor and evaluation of its performance and efficiency is also presented, and is verified on the Linux kernel 5.0. Fostered by advancements in processor architecture, T-Visor is capable of optimizing virtualization performance by directly interacting with hardware resources. 

Experimental results show that T-Visor achieves satisfactory performance and efficiency when used in conjunction with real-time applications under both Linux and uvisor operating systems. A comparative analysis of T-Visor and other existing approaches is presented, highlighting T-Visor's performance advantages. This research aims to promote hypervisor-based fault isolation and improve embedded real-time system security through hypervisor technology. T-Visor is made available as open-source software to support future research and development in this area.

T-Visor builds upon this concept by integrating new mechanisms to support mixed-importance embedded real-time systems.

Many significant advancements have been made in automatic panorama creation. This study instead explores the potential uses of the created panoramas in real-world applications, rather than the methods to create them. It is hypothesized that include contextual information such as a person's point of view when generating a panorama. This can be accomplished by first identifying the most important images in a panorama based on the inclination of the camera's axis. This can then be achieved through a series of mathematical transformations to analyze the orientation of the camera's axis and to calculate the most favorable viewing angle. This study demonstrates that incorporating contextual information enhances the user experience of the panorama. Furthermore, it is shown that a straightforward technique can effectively capture a person's point of view and can be utilized as a key component in panorama creation with minimal additional computations required. This technique can also be used to create personalized 360-degree videos by determining the most preferred viewing angles across various dimensions. It is shown that taking into account a person's point of view can aid in detecting irregularities in their preferred perspective and can aid in detecting cheating in immersive experiences. This study also investigates the potential applications of the created panoramas in psychological assessments. It is shown that analyzing the time spent viewing objects of different intrinsic values can effectively quantify a person's level of intrinsic motivation. Our findings also demonstrate that incorporating contextual information can help identify objects that hold intrinsic value by considering a person's past behaviors. The study showcases various practical uses of the created panoramas in significant application areas such as human-computer interaction, psychology, and behavior monitoring. The study's findings also highlight the significance of accounting for the context of the viewer in applications of panoramic photography.
