This research investigates the relationship between COVID-19 coverage in local U.S. news and its effects on infection and mortality rates, taking into account the characteristics of the audience. We construct a comprehensive dataset of TV news and COVID-19 metrics across 144 regions between April and July 2020. Notably, areas with greater news coverage had lower infection rates, yet regions focusing more on the topic actually saw higher mortality rates. What's more, audiences who watched more news were more likely located in regions with higher infection rates. Interestingly, stations owned by larger networks covered the pandemic less extensively than those owned by independent networks. Moreover, human-journalists versus robot-generated news showed distinct perspectives on the pandemic. We explore the implications of these findings and their potential connections to vaccination rates, which are still being researched. Ultimately, this study demonstrates a significant connection between journalism standards and a society's well-being.

The Rapid Multipole Algorithm is a highly efficient method for solving Vlasov equations in complex plasma simulations with limited spatial and velocity resolution. However, this method introduces small errors when calculating the force and potential fields due to approximating cell-based values, which can cause subtle impacts on macroscopic properties. Previous research revealed that these small errors don't affect conservation of total energy and linear momentum, but a theoretical study is needed to understand their effect on angular momentum conservation. Our study shows that the RMPS algorithm preserves total angular momentum, proving a long-held assumption, by quantifying the upper limit of error for each variable involved in its equations. Our research also highlights how these small errors contribute to momentum exchange between particles and the fluid. Our findings were validated through numerical experiments using plasmas with step functions as velocity profiles in various dimensions. Numerical data on energy and angular momentum confirm that RMPS preserves these quantities with minimal error, which correlates with our analytically derived limits. Additionally, simulations of non-interacting particles showed that RMPS maintains total angular momentum while introducing minimal error and preserves energy. These results can help in developing more accurate and advanced algorithms in this field. Our study also provides guidance on achieving real-time plasma simulations with both energy and angular momentum conservation. Furthermore, incorporating adaptive time-stepping was validated in simulations of a homogeneous isotropic vortex. Lastly, a 3D simulation of the Taylor-Goudas singularity was performed while demonstrating conservation of total angular momentum with minimal error. The observed results matched our analytically derived limits. Additionally, a comparison of energy conservation limits in this test case was performed. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the RMPS algorithm in plasma simulations. Its use in more efficient plasma simulations is demonstrated through a comparison with particle-in-cell methods. Moreover, a 3D simulation of the Bessel function velocity profile was performed while achieving real-time solution using the initial conditions from the test case of a homogeneous, isotropic vortex. Together, these results verify the accuracy of the RMPS algorithm in complex plasma simulations. They also demonstrate its efficient use in such cases. One particular demonstration of its use in such cases is in simulations of the Farley-Buneman instability. Medical specialists' images hold valuable information despite occasional errors in diagnosis. High-quality AI models can identify rare conditions in limited datasets. However, these models may incorrectly assign patterns from one specialist's images, affecting overall performance. This study finds that incorporating data augmentation is insufficient in preventing a model from replicating a specialist's patterns. We then propose the Balance for Inter-subject generalization using augmentation on features range (BIFR) method, which uses an entropy-based loss to balance the distribution of training features across multiple specialists, while also incorporating another augmentation method to balance the distribution within each specialist's images. The BIFR method is applied to an advanced cardiac disease dataset and compares performance with and without data augmentation, and an unbalanced control group. Results indicate that BIFR achieves better accuracy and/at set detection performance compared to both DAFR (with no augmentation) and the control group. This study is the first to evaluate DAFR on the AID dataset and extends the concept to multi-label conditions. It is found that localisation performance is better when considering both the positive and negative labels simultaneously. We propose the Balance for Inter-subject generalization using augmentation on labels range (BILR) method, which uses a step-loss to balance the distribution of positive and negative labels across specialists while using an additional method to balance the distribution within each specialist's images. The BILR method is applied to an Aid dataset with m=3 and n=2 and shows improved performance compared to a control group. It is also found that using an entropy-based classifier with no additional labels information is a simple way to improve the accuracy of an aid dataset. The proposed methods are tested and evaluated using a comprehensive experimental study. Analysis of the experiments shows that the proposed methods are supported by theoretical evidence and are feasible to implement. They are found to have a positive impact on the health sector by improving aid model generalisation and reducing errors in diagnosis. Finally, the proposed methods are presented at an international conference in 2021 under the names BIFR and BILR. The names BIFR and BILR are abbreviations for Balance for Inter-subject generalization using augmentation on features range and Balance for Inter-subject generalization using augmentation on labels range respectively. A detailed study of a specific interaction between two Higgs bosons and a vector boson has been conducted, utilizing 139 to 138 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data recorded at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider.  Higgs-Vector Boson Compositeness (HVBC) and Higgs-Pair Compositeness (HPC) parameters are introduced to restrict the complexity of the production process.  Observations of the three-particle system's cross-section are made for pairs of 125 GeV Higgs bosons and 125 GeV Higgs boson and vector boson combinations.  The calculated cross-sections for these observations are compared to standard model predictions.  The calculated and observed Higgs-Vector Boson Compositeness parameters are reported for all considered processes.  The probability of the calculated Higgs-Pair Compositeness parameters being consistent with the observed values is also determined for various complex terms.  This study provides the most precise measurement of $pp$ collision cross-sections for pairs of 125 GeV Higgs bosons and 125 GeV Higgs boson and vector boson combinations at 13 TeV, with observed and calculated cross-sections respectively ranging from 60 to 140 fb and 60 to 140 fb.  The calculated and observed Higgs-Pair Compositeness parameters for the primary considered process are within the range of -110 to 110 GeV^4,  -110 to 110 GeV^4 respectively.  This study utilizes Higgs-Pair Compositeness parameters for the first time.  The calculated limits on HVBC parameters for the production of two 125 GeV Higgs bosons are 2.2*10^8 TeV^4, and for the production of a 125 GeV Higgs boson and a vector boson are 2.5*10^8 TeV^4.  These limits are the most stringent experimental constraints on HVBC parameters for the considered production processes.  The study has excluded a specific region of the parameter space for models of 125 GeV Higgs boson couples to 125 GeV Higgs bosons or vector bosons with coupling constants of 0.3 or 0.6 for model types 2y2y and 2y2gamma respectively. The high sensitivity of masers makes them ideal tools for observing subthermal ensembles in both astrophysical objects and solid-state materials. A lack of thermal equilibrium is characteristic of certain systems, such as spin ensembles, where non-temperature distributions can be induced by various means. Theoretical models predict the existence of Alkaline Earth atoms with long-lived nuclear spin states, and a digital maser is proposed as a means to detect such ensembles through massive improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. A prototype digital maser has been developed, and a series of experiments have been conducted to test its sensitivity to multiple types of spin ensembles. A 10,000-fold enhancement in noise reduction has been achieved, and the system is currently being fine-tuned to enhance this capability even further. The Alkaline Earth system of choice is Be$^7$, featuring a long-lived $T_1$ relaxation time and a nuclear spin of $I=3/2$. The digital maser is being modified to detect this system, with expected improvements in sensitivity that could lead to its widespread use in astrophysical and solid-state research. The system is being tested in its current form, and a new phase of research is anticipated once it has achieved full capability. The planned system is being designed to operate at a level at which individual magnetic spin interactions could potentially be detected individually, rather than through ensemble-averaged collections. The system is being developed with a view to applying it not only to astrophysical objects and solid-state materials but also to biological systems with long-lived spin states. The latter is seen as particularly significant given the potential for magnetic resonance imaging to reveal sub-thermal ensembles in the body. A genus calculation method is proposed for thick graphs, which involves transforming the graph into a surface-topological structure called a compact surface-category, then determining the minimum number of times the assigned identity elements intersect in order to embed the graph's skeleton onto a 2-dimensional surface. Although this approach provides a straightforward solution, it does involve some computationally intensive operations. Nevertheless, it can be optimized by breaking down the graph into simpler components called linked cycles, solving each component independently, and then consolidating the results. This revised method reduces the computational complexity and makes the genus calculation more efficient in practical terms. Additionally, we provide some example use cases where this algorithm is applied. Furthermore, we offer some general insights on enhancing algorithms for finding spanning surfaces. Finally, the efficiency of the proposed method is compared with existing solutions via empirical testing. The research underlying this study was initially presented at a conference in Moscow in 2017. This paper focuses on solving the distributed average consensus problem for a group of nodes, where each node $i$ receives input vector $x_i$ and an objective function function $f_i(\cdot)$ that it aims to minimize by optimizing its local variable $x_i$. A decentralized algorithm is designed to allow nodes to communicate with their neighbors through a limited bandwidth connection. A randomized Newton method is developed to achieve the highest possible level of scalability, where each node $i$ calculates its derivative and Hessian matrix for $f_i(\cdot)$ before using the obtained information to update its local variable $x_i$. By leveraging the properties of a complex exponential signal, a novel method is constructed to ensure that the calculated variable values for each node are aggregated across the group while maintaining stability. A comprehensive theoretical analysis is conducted to verify the effectiveness of this method in achieving the optimal solution of the distributed average consensus problem. Simulated experiments are performed to support the obtained results. Furthermore, an extension of this algorithm is also provided to handle the issue of an incomplete Hessian matrix for the objective functions. Although this additional method does not guarantee the optimal communication efficiency, it is verified to be effective through theoretical and experimental studies. Comprehensive numerical simulations are used to evaluate its performance, where notable results are highlighted in the experimental section. A thorough comparison with a distributed gradient method is also performed, where experimental outcomes are used to answer the question of which method is suitable for different types of performance requirements and provide insights for future research in this area. When working with machine learning models, an important consideration is how their outputs are viewed and understood by different people, including experts in various fields. To address this, a team of researchers has been studying the viewing contexts of machine-generated outputs, which can impact how these messages are perceived by experts in specific domains. This paper focuses on the challenge of tagging contextual cues for fair assessment of commercial driving abilities. To overcome this, a dual-specialist setup is proposed, consisting of a linguistic expert and a domain-expert, who respectively identify contextual signals and interpret machine-generated outputs in the context of specific domains. To streamline this process, a method of combining dual-specialist inputs is presented, using clustering to integrate their inputs. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study on a video sharing platform, where a linguistic specialist and a specialist for commercial driving content worked together to tag and interpret machine-generated outputs. The experimental results show that the proposed framework successfully captures contextual information and comprehensible human meanings. The complete implementation of this workflow, including the key tools and data, is available for immediate use on the HuggingFace Hub. The direct link to the repository is provided. To evaluate the proposed method, a small-scale experiment was conducted, which showed that it performed comparably to a large pre-trained language model in terms of accuracy for the fair assessment task, but the method is computationally more efficient and offers more transparent human understanding. To further validate the approach, a usability experiment was also carried out, which highlighted several key benefits, including the ability to provide nuanced and complex human understanding, the ability to accommodate diverse commercial driving expertise, and the ability to produce outputs that are relevant and useful for the specific domain. The study also uncovered several usability issues, such as the need for more clear and interactive tagging of contextual signals and the need for more detailed and context-dependent interpretation of machine-generated outputs. To address these challenges, future work is suggested. Ultimately, the proposed method and associated findings have significant implications for a range of practical applications where expert knowledge is essential for the safe and effective interaction between humans and machines. As such, this research is an important step towards creating more equitable and understandable machine learning systems that benefit society as a whole. To this end, a set of practical recommendations for developers, researchers, and users is provided. This paper presents a challenge called the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge (OOLC) held at IJCAI 2020, where participants worked to improve the accuracy of Machine Translation by generating words outside a given vocabulary. The challenge aimed to simulate real-life scenarios in which MT systems encounter unfamiliar words. Specifically, the problem was framed using an extended version of the NMT model to translate both in-lexicon and out-of-lexicon words. The challenge featured a benchmarking platform and a data set comprised of two parts: a signal-free subset for automatic evaluation and a signal-rich subset for manual assessment. Four methods were proposed to tackle this issue, with the simplest being a conventional replacement approach using unknown word symbols. Other methods involved replacing unknown words with equivalents, including one unknown word, two unknown words, or a sequence of unknown words. The results showed that using unknown word sequences slightly outperformed the other methods. Additionally, a hard unknown word model that maps unknown words to a 'HARD' token was explored in conjunction with the other methods. The challenge also encompassed a companion analysis, a case study, and a set of comprehensive experiments that revealed further insights into this problem. A novel geometric approach is developed to analyze temporal evolution of parametric Gaussian stochastic systems by inferring the underlying geometric structure of the parameter space. The approach can either treat the space as a traditional Riemannian manifold or alternatively, with irregularities acknowledged, as a space with Gaussian stochastic fields, utilizing novel definitions of differentiation and the geodesic equation. By exploring the latter, the study finds closed forms of the shortest paths in selected one- and two-dimensional parameter spaces. Additionally, a numerical method is proposed to approximate geodesics in higher dimensional spaces. The approximate geodesic geometry is applied to optimize the performance of Gaussian-based surrogates for expensive parametric PDEs. We also contribute a (stochastic) Newton-Kantorovich theorem to define a localization notion and a novel criterion to assess the convergence of geodesic approximation. By analyzing the criteria for convergence and locality, this study defines criteria to identify irregularities in Gaussian stochastic fields, enabling the determination of the geometric structure and the approximation quality. Case studies, involving both PDE and Hamiltonian-based applications, demonstrate the proposed methods' effectiveness. A set of exact solutions has been derived for ideal fluid warp spacetimes that also account for a possible cosmological constant.  These exact solutions, represented by the Alcubierre, ideal fluid - cosmological constant Schwarzschild, and ideal fluid - cosmological constant Treser, have been computed analytically and numerically, effectively transforming the nonlinear partial differential equations into a set of ordinary differential equations that form an Cauchy problem.  In the numerically obtained warp spacetimes, a key feature is a matter density profile that is positive in the core and negative at the edges, fulfilling the condition set by the Tolman-Ehrenfest equation, thus allowing for a theoretical basis for warp drive engineering.  Additionally, in the numerically derived warp spacetimes, a "dumb hole" phenomenon is observed, similar to that seen in a black hole, and a "warp bubble" expands in a manner consistent with the light cone in flat spacetime. The shift to smart and sustainable cities accelerates the development of diverse urban infrastructures. Managing extensive networks of underground structures such as power, water, gas, and transportation requires highly efficient mapping, assessment, and planning tools. While GIS technology advanced, it failed to integrate adequately with these networks, leading to the emergence of new data models and technologies. This thesis introduces the GUIDES framework, a knowledge-based system for mapping and managing underground and above-ground infrastructures using a BIM data model and a integrated front-end system. It showcases its potential through a practical implementation on the city of Sofia. This research aims to contribute the GUIDES framework, demonstrating its usefulness through a real-world case scenario. The outcome aims to inspire future developments and improvements, resulting in the creation of a new open-source city engineering platform. The primary goal of this research is to aid in the effective management and mapping of a smart and sustainable city's infrastructures. The initial real-world implementation of the GUIDES framework has already been achieved, and it is now proposed to advance the concept further by making it accessible as a public cloud service. The study behind this research was conducted at the Advanced Information Systems and Communications Laboratory at the School of Engineering of the University of West Attica. The primary researcher responsible for this study is Georgi Y. Yovchev. The presentation provided key details about the GUIDES framework, including its purpose, models, deployment, and initial results. The next part of the presentation dels with the actual implementation of the GUIDES metropolitan model. The presentation concludes by outlining the future plans for the GUIDES model and service, namely integrating it as a layer in geographic information systems used in Greece. The presentation also touches upon the integration of the GUIDES model with other cities in Greece and abroad. The final part is dedicated to discussing the future plans of the GUIDES service, including demonstrating it at the European Urbanist Congress. The main strength of the GUIDES framework lies in its ability to efficiently process queries, particularly those involving the assessment of 3D relationships between the infrastructures it contains. Originally, this capability was developed and tested on a model of the underground power networks in Sofia. The presentation also outlines the process of rendering the 3D representations of the networks, including the creation of the necessary metadata. The main goals of this research are to provide accurate 3D representations of the networks and enable planning using game engines. This research explores the feasibility of leveraging multiple, parallel interactive sessions to improve model performance, even when faced with errors resulting from either user or model bias. This first involves developing an iterative approach to reconstructing the program the model intends to generate, based on assessment feedback provided by the user. A novel Bayesian reconstruction method is introduced that utilizes Gaussian Processes to infer the probability distribution of the model's program state. This method serves as a noise-reducing filter, enabling the reconstruction of a refined state that more accurately reflects the model's performance over time. This assessment reliability is then utilized as a form of feedback regularization during the state reconstruction process, thereby improving the method's overall effectiveness. Users interact more effectively with graphical representations than raw time series data because static visuals convey additional information. Nonetheless, dynamic visuals only offering motion over time lack this benefit. To address this, we developed "time seeker," a drag-and-drop interaction that enables users to identify correlations between time-based features in time series data, similar to how users correlate attributes in multidimensional data displays. We optimized this interaction for linear data, proposing heap views to showcase all relevant time instants, and heap highlights to display key moments. User studies showed that time seeker outperformed comparable interactions in tasks involving feature correlations and forecasting. Additionally, user preferences were found in how information is presented and retrieved. We found time seeker to be beneficial in various domains including weather, music, and network traffic analysis. Our work integrates time series exploration and forecasting, providing a solution to a long-standing challenge in human-computer interaction. The behavior of an electric double layer at the boundary of a charged soft interface is investigated using a mean-field approach. The system under investigation consists of a mixture of two solvents and an electrolyte, with a membrane that is either neutral or slightly charged in a first-order mean-field theory. The effects of solvent polarization on the interfacial properties are analyzed through a parameter, representing the difference in charge transfer capabilities of the solvents. The outcome reveals nontrivial interfacial profiles and density profiles that depend on the degree of solvent polarization, particularly in the presence of a monolayer charge regime. Additionally, the interfacial potential and charge in such a system are found to decrease as the difference in charge transfer capabilities increases, whereas a balancing effect on these properties is observed in a high coupling regime. Furthermore, the system's properties are compared to those of a mixture of identical solvents with specific ion sizes. The results indicate non-ideal conditions in both cases, with varying degrees of non-ideality depending on the model parameters and the degree of solvent polarization. Finally, the effects of applied potential on the interfacial properties are investigated, with results showing that the interfacial potential increases with increasing potential, whereas the double-layer width decreases and eventually vanishes as the interfacial charge approaches its asymptotic value. The outcome reveals complex and non-ideal behavior of the system, with dependencies on the degree of solvent polarization, ion sizes, and applied potential. The obtained results are discussed in the context of relevant experimental and application backgrounds. With this model, the effects of solvent polarization on the interfacial properties can be explored, potentially providing valuable insights for understanding various processes at the boundary of soft interfaces, with implications for technologies involving ionically charged soft interfaces. The work is relevant to a wide range of applications, including biomembranes, nanofluidics, energy storage, and energy conversion. The study paves the way for understanding and modeling various physical and biological systems, with a potential extension to include nonequilibrium approaches and more realistic systems for soft interfaces. The relevance of the work to biological systems is also discussed, with specific examples of applications to cellular membranes and biosensors. The work contributes significantly to understanding and modeling electrolyte systems, with results that can be applied to a wide range of soft and biological interfaces. The relevant theory and models can be used to design and engineer systems for nanofluidics and energy storage, with implications for understanding various processes at the boundary of soft and biological interfaces. Discovering software requirements from unstructured text proofreads poses a significant challenge, as existing methods often struggle to understand the context. To address this difficulty, our approach diverges from conventional state-of-the-art techniques and instead views requirement discovery as a problem of specifying system behavior through input-output relationships. By utilizing machine learning to recognize these input-output connections in text, our method effectively identifies system behaviors and constructs specifications. We introduce a novel technique called Text2Spec, which incorporates neural networks to generate formal descriptions for found requirements. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a case study and a set of experiments comparing Text2Spec with existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our study highlights common errors in existing approaches and clarifies the distinct capabilities of these algorithms, revealing that some are more effective at understanding context than others. While Text2Spec shows promising results, it performs poorly on new, unseen data, suggesting opportunities for future research to improve its robustness. This technique incorporates relay nodes in the network to lower the transmission bandwidth requirements of the source node and make the network more efficient by allowing the source node to turn off its transmitters when not in use. The technique involves two main time slots - one for data transmission and another for configuration and control processes. The source node and relay nodes are active during the data transmission slot, and during the configuration and control slot, the source node and relay nodes are inactive, allowing the receipt of control signals from the destination to the source and relay nodes. The source node uses this information to adjust its encoding method to make the transmission in the next data transmission slot more band-width efficient. The technique requires two time slots, however it does not need to be repeated consecutively, and several consecutive data transmission slots can co-occur with a single configuration and control slot, significantly reducing the energy consumption by the source node. The technique combines the transmission scheduling of the source and relay nodes with the scheduling of the power distribution in the network. The technique minimizes the total power consumed by the source and relay nodes by taking into account the band-width requirements for each transmission round and relating it to the power requirements for each transmission round to obtain an optimal trade-off between band-width efficiency and energy consumption, thus lowering overall energy consumption by the source node and relay nodes. The technique combines optimisation in distributed encoding, relay placement, and power distribution stages to obtain a refined candidate solution. The technique reduces band-width consumption while lowering overall energy consumption by the source node and relay nodes. Our research focuses on addressing prejudice in software development, specifically
by investigating potential biases introduced during code copy-paste, and how to
detect and prevent it. To address this issue, we have developed two solutions:
 Firstly, a novel metric to measure distribution-to-distribution distance has been
introduced, enabling accurate comparison of different code distributions with a
high degree of precision. Secondly, an artificial intelligence-powered filter
has been created to automatically identify and remove potential bias from code
when compared or aligned across different distributions. Results from testing
indicate the AI-powered filter is highly effective, correctly identifying and
excluding 94% of prejudice cases. To further address this issue, our team is
shifting focus to prejudice detection and prevention, leveraging supervised
machine learning to build a model capable of accurately identifying and
understanding prejudice. This work marks a significant first effort in
addressing prejudice within the context of software diversity, and we believe
this research will open new avenues for exploring software prejudice as a field
of study. To facilitate replication and advancement, our code and data have been
made publicly available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/

diversity, our research aims to establish key concepts and techniques for
addressing prejudice, and we invite others to join this effort and drive

research aims to establish prejudice as a recognized concept within the
technical community, leading to improved practices and a culture of diversity
in software development. A corresponding paper was presented at the 2022
International Conference on Software Diversity. A comprehensive tutorial on

HAXES, a high-energy x-ray absorption fine structure technique, offers unique insights into the electronic states of bulk and bulk-like materials at the nanoscale. Its complex measurements involve numerous data processing steps, leading to a straightforward physical interpretation. A rate-based model is proposed to simplify the multi-step electronic relaxation process during HAXES experiments. Utilizing this model, the evolution of photoexcited electron groups over time can be tracked and represented in the form of time-dependent propagators. Simulations, based on standard electron-phonon coupling parameters, show that the relaxation occurs rapidly within a few picoseconds, with the model also accurately replicating experimental outcomes for a variety of materials. Furthermore, the model's validity was established by simulating iron's high-energy absorption spectrum at various temperatures and finding a strong correlation with existing studies. A direct relationship between the electron groups' rate parameters and the material's bulk properties makes them valuable tools for studying the physical properties of materials at the nanoscale and beyond. A corresponding Python package is provided to facilitate the simulation and data analysis of HAXES measurements, which is particularly beneficial for real-time simulations and data-driven studies. A future application of this model is to analyze time-resolved HAXES measurements, allowing the distinction of different relaxation mechanisms that occur on a similar timescale. A proposed future experiment could investigate the bulk properties of diamond, a temperature-controlled environment. By analyzing the time-integrated and time-resolved HAXES measurements, the model can distinguish between bulk and surface-scene-specific electron relaxation, leading to valuable insights into the material's bulk and surface properties. In advanced simulations, creating diverse radiation signature profiles can pose difficulties for development and training, particularly for medical device classification using GAN. To overcome this, researchers previously employed adversarial training against faulty GANs to create stable models, but their approach was specifically designed for medical device classification and required prior knowledge of classification architectures. This study presents a novel training method, the blend GAN, utilizing multiple GANs to improve the resilience of pre-trained models against hostile adversarial attacks without requiring prior knowledge of the model's details. This approach is particularly demonstrated with the task of radiation modulation classification, which involves generating classification models using GANs for different types of radiation signatures. The effectiveness of the blend GAN approach is evaluated against standard adversarial training methods, using radiation signature and gamma source data, to classify the embedded items within samples. The results indicate a significant improvement in the robustness of the GAN models, with minimal deterioration in dice coefficients and segmentation watermark robustness when subjected to adversarial attacks, whereas adversarial training alone showed limited benefits. Furthermore, an analysis of the implications for radiation source categorization revealed that the blend GAN approach allows for accurate source type identification even in the presence of hostile attacks. This study contributes to the creation of medical device classification models with enhanced resilience against hostile adversarial attacks, which can be crucial in applications such as radiation source classification. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions in EMIs can be challenging due to similarities in CSF and White Matter tissues. Most approaches rely on supervised learning, using datasets from a single source. Given the limited training data and unique characteristics of EMIs, patients' datasets often need to be segmented individually, a labor-intensive process due to the lack of public datasets. Rigid and transferable features, common in medical imaging, make it difficult for models to generalize. Instead of relying on similar-sized datasets, we explore the potential of continuous learning through disease progression and biopsy-based segmentation as a more effective approach for initial segmentation, before the development of accurate automated models. Biopsies serve as perfect benchmarks for testing segmentation algorithms, offering distinct tissue distribution in various diseases. Moreover, the increased presence of GS in biopsies allows for improved supervision of segmentation algorithms. We introduce a novel approach, incorporating U-Net-based microglia training, continuous learning in patient histories, and biopsy-based supervision of lesion segmentation. Biopsies' ability to assess lesions locally and histopathologically inspected cavities may provide significant insights, leading to accurate lesion segmentation in EMIs. We also introduce a new, extensive biopsy-based lesion segmentation dataset, BiMSL, comprising 1222 lesions, as the first of its kind to combine multiple clinics into a comprehensive resource for the medical imaging community. The proposed method, initially applied to the BiMSL dataset, significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms, even when the model is transferred to the patient's clinical dataset from the same source. Most notably, this study also showcases the model’s ability to handle new clinical datasets from different sources, eventually achieving superior performance compared to the initial supervised approach. Moreover, the study's results demonstrate the effectiveness of continuous learning in models that handle the progression of various diseases such as Multiple Sclerosis, even when the model is applied to a new modality, biopsy, with minimal need for additional training. The maniac classifier is a straightforward, white-box inspection tool designed to detect potential issues in machine learning models, particularly those involving unfair biases in classification. Its core functionality allows the examination of how much the predicted class labels of a trained model change when training inputs are modified slightly. By analyzing these slight modifications, the maniac classifier can identify and flag instances where a model exhibits unfair bias, which can arise due to patterns present in the training data or biases that are inherent in the system itself. Initially validated on a simplified binary classification problem, the maniac classifier was also tested and performed well on a selection of fair and biased datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in uncovering biases in trained machine learning models. Furthermore, the maniac classifier can be used to identify and flag biases based on specific characteristics of interest, such as protected characteristics, thus promoting the creation of fair machine learning models that are in line with regulatory requirements. With its ease of use and fair results, the maniac classifier provides a reliable tool for conducting unbiased training, which is particularly beneficial in scenarios where institutions have a legal or ethical obligation to avoid model biases. Currently, the maniac classifier supports training and testing data in the form of images, but it can be modified to handle other data types, such as text and tabular data, though this may require additional processing of the input data. Training data can take the form of hand-labeled information or unambiguous outputs from other models, while testing data can be provided by human labels or known instances of high-confidence, ground-truth classifications. Testing data do not need to be complete, as the maniac classifier can flag instances where a model's classification is ambiguous or certain. Similarly, the training data do not need to be comprehensive, as the maniac classifier can flag instances of strong bias even if the training data is incomplete. Training data can be as simple as a list of classes and corresponding ground-truth labels, which the maniac classifier uses to define the boundary spaces for each class. Additionally, the maniac classifier supports multi-label data, where each instance can have multiple classes, which can help to identify potential biases related to class distributions. As a lightweight tool with minimal computational requirements, the maniac classifier can be easily adapted for use on small datasets, which can be written in any programming language. For image data, the maniac classifier can be used with a standard library such as Pillow, which provides support for image manipulation. A proposed explanation is that set augmentation introduces contextual dependencies that are at odds with the intrinsic relationships within images. A theoretical framework involving preference relations is used to further study the effects of contextual and non-contrastive relationships. This framework provides a method to evaluate the quality of representations using preference relations. Polymer glass transition dynamics can be complicated by numerous factors at
different scales, including the effects of individual molecules, intermolecular
interactions, and a broad array of cluster sizes. By analyzing these factors in
relation to each other, research has shown that the onset of slow motion in
polymers involves a critical temperature threshold, which varies depending on
the specific molecule or cluster observed. This threshold is particularly
sensitive to the smallest scales, becoming more intense and shifted towards higher
temperatures as the observation scale increases. Consequently, interpreting
experimental results from various scales demands caution to avoid misleading
conclusions regarding the overall dynamics of the system. Furthermore, our
research highlights important similarities and connections between methods
focusing on identifying homogeneous and heterogeneous aspects of the dynamics. 
Despite apparent differences, they both stem from the application of
entropy-driven principles that underpin the thermodynamic properties of the
system. This integration of thermodynamic and dynamic observations provides a
more unified understanding of the early stages of glass formation. It can be
applied not only to synthetic polymer systems, which were the focus of our
previous studies, but also to natural biopolymers and other systems where
water interacts with simple or large molecular substances to create a complex
hydrogen bond network. This broader scope includes systems like hydrogels,
proteins, and related solutions where the emergence of a liquid-liquid phase
transition might contribute to the development of new materials and therapies. 
By combining ideas inspired by de Gennes' concept of the homogeneity
principle, our analysis demonstrates that the thermodynamic and dynamic
properties of systems undergoing a glass transition are interconnected through
a multistage process, which can be viewed as a multi-faceted ribbons network
formed by the overlap of various intermolecular and molecular monolayers.

Children constantly learn new words and integrate them into their vocabulary, but sometimes they may encounter words that are rejected due to incorrect syntax or meaning.  Although there is substantial research on how adults process language, there is limited study on children's language rejection and the strategies they employ to ignore incorrect words.  To simulate children's language rejection and the ways they learn to avoid incorrect words, we developed two novel methods.  We integrated an acceptance/in rejection decision-making process into two established transformer models, transforming them into GReD-LM models that can select between accepted and rejected words.  Our approach is the first to use machine learning to effectively model children's language rejection and response to non-responsive words.  Using two existing databases, we trained these models and evaluated them on two tasks: selecting correct words in incorrect options, and ignoring incorrect words.  The results show that the proposed models successfully recognize the likelihood of a word being rejected and effectively choose the correct word in situations with multiple incorrect options.  Furthermore, the rejected word models developed in this study are the first to use machine learning to identify unresponsive words in children's language and effectively ignore them, opening up new avenues for research on children's language development.  We believe that these models, once perfected, could play a crucial part in the creation of AI systems capable of interacting with children naturally.  In addition, we provide access to our source code, data, and results on http://grendl-m.com.  An additional file: Video Appendix.pdf lists our relevant research conferences and meetings.  Specifically, we presented our findings at the following events:  AML2019, ITiCSE-SPOC2019, ICM2020, SIGCHI2020, EMNLP2020, CHI2021. When analyzing open-ended creative text such as fiction, understanding generation strategies is particularly crucial. Research indicates readers often focus on specific aspects of the story, yet existing visualizations of generation processes in neural models fail to mirror this focused approach. We introduce a novel method aimed at revealing the sequential nature of neural model decision-making processes during the generation of creative text. By seamlessly embedding a 'look-ahead focus' mechanism in the model, we capture detailed representations of the output state and focus on relevant parts to guide the model's subsequent actions, much like human readers. We develop a 'eye-movement' analysis for the generated output, representing the model's internal focus at each step as it enables or disables specific actions. Experimental results on the NARRATIVE dataset reveal our method achieves an accurate prediction of the model's focus in 51% of the cases, exceeding the 33% accuracy achieved by blind evaluation without utilizing the model's internal state. Moreover, we observe the model's decision-making processes demonstrate a 'goal-oriented' pattern, with goal types including'storytelling,' 'description,' and 'exploration.' The work presents a new framework for studying goal-oriented learning in neural machine interpretation and offers fresh insights into the models' decision-making processes, linking them to the focused approaches employed by human readers during the analysis of creative text. Unfortunately, the method relies heavily on specific properties of the geometric distribution, which are not inherent in all Markov processes. Furthermore, the approach assumes a fundamental understanding of the Markov-driven Asian model (MDA), but this assumption may not always hold. In fact, pricing complex Asians under stochastic interest rates and multiple physical risks is an open problem. In their original paper, Li and Ng actually demonstrated the feasibility of extending the MDA to the Cai model, which includes time-varying parameters in the geometric distribution. Consequently, the claimed universality of their method in Li and Ng (2021) is unlikely. In contrast, we provide a novel approximation framework for a broad class of Asian options, which does not presuppose any understanding of the M.

In this work, we present a novel approximation framework for a broad class of Asian options, which does not require knowledge of the underlying probability distribution. Our approximation method is based on two key components: a discounted sum representation of a standard Asian option and a dynamic partial averaging technique. In numerical experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for pricing multiple types of Asian options, which outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Notably, our approximation method achieves high precision with a small number of simulation iterations and a minimal amount of computation time. In theoretical analysis, we establish the precision and computational complexity of our approximation method. In a comparative analysis, we evaluate the performance of the proposed approximation method and other state-of-the-art approaches, revealing that it significantly outperforms existing standards in terms of accuracy and computational speed. In fact, our approximation method is found to be at least two times faster than the best available method in Li and Ng (2021), which outperformed other approaches in their original study. In practical applications, the proposed approximation method is found to be versatile, allowing it to price a wide variety of Asian options and options baskets and generate real-time quotes in high-frequency trading environments. In sum, the proposed approximation method is found to be fast, efficient, and versatile in pricing various types of Asian options and options portfolios. In conventional cosmological collider physics, massive particles produced in the early universe can be studied by observing their distinctive, non-thermal features in the universe's present-day relic density. We explore an alternative scenario where the universe's initial conditions are unknown and instead focus on a universal, thermal background. A new paradigm emerges, known as "initial features," where the presence of these unique features indicates the existence of heavy, massive particles. These features differ from traditional non-thermal reliefs in that they can arise from any massless, long-lived intermediate particle and are characteristic of both thermal and non-thermal production processes. By examining the relic density and its momentum space distribution, we demonstrate the potential to differentiate between various production mechanisms, including for the first time, initial features generated through self-interactions. Finally, we examine the potential for next-generation cosmological observations to reveal the signature of a universal initial feature. This signature could be detected at a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 0.1 with a 10-year mission using the Cosmic Inflation Survey, thus offering a new possibility for probing the universe's very early stages. Moreover, in the context of Higgs collider physics, where the universe's initial feature is frozen into the relic density and momentum distribution below the Higgs rest mass, we find that it can be distinguished from thermal distribution at the 10$\%$ level with a 10-year mission. These findings highlight the promise of identifying the universe's initial feature with remarkable implications for our understanding of physics beyond the Standard Model. The method of distinguishing massless particles' features at the accuracy of 0.1, achieved through a 10-year mission, can be applied broadly across Standard Model extensions and is compatible with existing cosmological bounds, with applications including the study of dark matter and inflation. Importantly, in all cases, the method results in the improvement of mass bounds, with the specific values depending on the particular model being considered. In general, for any particle with a coupling to radiation, the method allows for the extension of its allowed mass range by a factor of $10^2$; for particles with a coupling to matter, including dark matter, its allowed mass range can be increased by a factor of $10^3$ or more, with the specific mass range depending on the assumed dark matter density. These findings indicate that the cosmic relic density can serve as a powerful probe of the universe's very early stages, with the cosmic feature providing a well-motivated and model-independent signature that can be used to test and refine

Convolutional neural networks, the cornerstone of image recognition, rely on spatial and feature pooling to overcome the complexities of large image dimensions, but the specifics of how they learn high-level features remain unclear. Our research reveals that convolutional networks learn object-specific features rather than general statistics of image subsets, contradicting long-held assumptions. To explain this, we introduce the latent visual-semantics filter focus, a framework that accounts for the effects of spatial and feature pooling. Our findings lead to the development of an efficient, error-reducing algorithm based on this concept. Moreover, we demonstrate that convolutional networks tend to prioritize distinguishing features, resulting in objects being represented by unique but non-distinguishable features, a phenomenon referred to as feature filter focus collapse. This issue is found to be both a strength and a weakness: while the capacity to ignore irrelevant features enhances generalisation, it also hampers an convolutional network's ability to distinguish between objects. Our research focuses on understanding the internal workings of a machine learning architecture, considered essential knowledge for informing model selection and design. As such, our work has significant implications for a range of fields, including diagnostic, the creation of artificial intelligence artists and other generative models, and the development of next-generation computer vision systems. To facilitate model selection, we describe a technique for visualizing and evaluating feature representations, as well as a method for scoring a network's capacity to distinguish between objects. For informative next-generation computer vision, we propose a network design that leverages part-based training, resulting in a model capable of distinguishing between objects, despite spatial and feature pooling. Moreover, we empirically demonstrate a network's ability to develop a spatial feature map, representing an organisation of semantic elements. To facilitate the creation of artificial intelligence artists and other generative models, we develop a framework for visualising decision-making processes. This framework is based on a novel approach to understanding decision trees, retaining axiomatic properties while providing a more interpretable representation of decision-making processes. This concept is found to be applicable in a range of contexts, including decision trees, neural networks, and other computationally complex models. For example, we describe a technique for visualising decision-making processes in the context of part-based neural networks. Our framework is applicable in a range of contexts, including computer vision and other domains requiring hierarchical understanding. This work has significant implications for informing model selection and design, considered essential knowledge for a range of fields. To facilitate the creation of diagnostic systems, we describe a technique for scoring a network's capacity to generalise.

This study proposes a new method of causal learning using an innovative
conceptual design approach. The objective is to discover the causal relationships
between variables in order to generate hypothetical scenarios. A case study was
carried out to test the feasibility of learning causal relationships from a dataset
containing operational data, which was compiled from a large-scale industrial
system. By applying various data preprocessing techniques, the system was
evaluated to assess the strength and validity of causal relationships between
variables. An innovative causal network representation was introduced to encode
causal connections, utilizing time-series data to determine the causal strength
of variables. The results of this study indicate that it is possible for operators to
utilize causal information to inform decision-making, with the added benefit of not
requiring domain expertise. A user-friendly interface was developed to present
causal connections and scenarios in a user-friendly manner, via a mobile
application or desktop interface. The system was successfully tested with
maintenance personnel, with the overall assessment being that the concept is
grounded in theory and has practical potential for implementation. Further
research will focus on refining the method and exploring applications to a
broader range of domains. A user-centered approach will also be adopted to
assess the impact of presenting causal information to operators and make
recommendations for improvement. Ultimately, the goal is to integrate the
system directly into the process monitoring and control interface, enabling
operators to leverage the benefits of causal information during operational
decisions. Key words: Conceptual process modeling, Causal learning, Inference
engineering, Industrial datasets, Data-driven approach, Conceptual design.

Our ab-initio calculations indicate that these structural distortions lead to the appearance of metastable states, known as magnetic skyrmions, through the application of magnetic field and field decrease. The dynamics of multiple grid-like structures of magnetic skyrmions is investigated as the system becomes stable under various structural transformations. Our results show that the movement of the skyrmion lattice as a whole can be manipulated by adjusting the structural distortions, without influencing the individual skyrmions' dynamics. This suggests the presence of a topologically-driven effect, dubbed 'topological liquefaction', which enables the control of the structural changes and corresponding magnetic properties during the transformation process. A comparable analogy can be drawn between this phenomenon and the change of state in Co$_{3}$Sn$_{2}$S$_{2}$ from a helical to a skyrmion configuration. The potential applications of Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn$_{2}$ are considered in the context of advanced technology, such as micro- and nano-scale data storage, which could potentially be improved by combining it with the recent discoveries of Co$_{3}$Sn$_{2}$S$_{2}$. Lastly, the possibility of realizing multiple topological states in the system through the application of electric and magnetic field is also explored. The results demonstrate that the structural relationships and corresponding magnetic properties of Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn$_{2}$ can be understood by considering the free energy minimization in the presence of structural distortions. The presence of multiple minima in the energy landscape suggests the possibility of different topological states, which could be manipulated by adjusting the structural distortions. The results of our study indicate that the structural relationships among various states can be deciphered by analyzing the symmetry of the structural distortions. The present research highlights the significance of structural distortions in shaping magnetic properties and opens up possibilities for further exploration of topological states through structural adjustments. The potential applications of structural adjustments in the context of topological states are vast and could lead to advancements in technologies such as data storage, which could also potentially improve our understanding of materials with existing properties. Lastly, we identify essential research directions that are crucial for further exploring and understanding HDLMs in their various forms. 
The research directions we present focus on theoretical developments, such as statistical representation, liquidation, and validation, as well as HDLMs' practical application and implementation. 
In practice, HDLMs face challenges such as noise, limited data, non-stationarity, non-linearity, interdependent events, and the inherent complexity of high-dimensional data.

Ultimately, we identify essential requirements for making practical advancements in this field: large-scale data analytics capabilities supported by cutting-edge computational tools. 
The future of HDLMs depends on finding the right balance between the complexity of the models and the characteristics of the data at hand.

As such, future research should prioritize the development of a unified framework that integrates different HDLM types and enables systematic evaluations of their effectiveness in various scenarios. 
Only through systematic evaluation and implementation can we gain a deeper understanding of the strengths and limitations of HDLMs and their practical potential in diverse domains.

The Balancing Domain Decomposition Method (BDDM) is a highly effective technique used to tackle the issues of oscillation and solution failure that may arise when using iterative methods like Conjugate Gradient (CG) to solve sparse systems. This is because CG, when applied to unsymmetrically conditioned matrices, can lead to slow convergence or even failure due to rounding errors. BDDM involves splitting a domain into smaller sub-domains and using a preconditioner that enforces continuity across these sub-domains. This approach has been shown to significantly improve convergence and solution accuracy. A key aspect of BDDM is the concept of balance, which requires that the residual within each sub-domain be close to the interface. This thesis explores a novel approach, introducing a static point method to address the balancing requirement. This method, inspired by the General Balance Domain Decomposition Method (GBDDM), uses a representative point within each sub-domain to assess balance and has been shown to guarantee positive definiteness, fast convergence, and solution uniqueness. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated through theoretical analysis and empirical testing. Notably, the static point method outperforms GBDDM in practice, offering a more efficient and scalable alternative. The proposed method can be seamlessly integrated with sparse direct solvers to solve large systems. Through numerical evaluations, it has been shown that the method can effectively handle a wide range of problems, including homogeneous and non-homogeneous systems, as well as H-matrices and double precision matrices. The method's superior performance is particularly evident in cases where local balance is challenging, such as with high aspect ratio sub-domains. Overall, the static point method has been shown to provide superior solution quality and efficiency compared to existing balancing methods, making it a valuable tool for tackling complex mathematical systems. A novel steganographic method known as U reversible steganography employs an encoder-decoder network architecture. We improve upon the existing U approach by implementing a Bayesian Neural Network framework. The Bayesian approach to U networks enhances their ability to conceal information while maintaining the integrity of the data. We experiment with different uncertainty representations, including the mean and standard deviation of output probabilities, and the predictive distribution of labels, to understand their impact on steganographic performance. The analysis of these representations reveals that the predictive distribution of labels offers the superior results, outperforming the current U method in both steganographic quality and achieving reversible results. An added benefit of this method is the potential to detect generated data through the standard deviation of predictive distributions, making it useful for detecting generated data. Our research reveals that the refined framework outperforms other top-ranked models, including those utilising pre-trained models and soft matching algorithms. This paper introduces a novel concept called polynomials perpendicular with a logarithmic burden, which derives from discrete equilibrium problems on weighted graphs. A central idea explored in this study is the asymptotic behavior of theorems surrounding logarithmic burden polynomials as the weighted graph's size increases. A model problem examined in detail involves a weighted line with a constant weight and uniformly distributed lengths, which demonstrates increasing rigidity as the size of the model expands. A primary discovery made through this example involves the asymptotic behavior of the polynomials in question, which was theoretically justified via a previously established convergence theory for complex functions under Dirichlet norms. This study builds upon two pivotal works: a study on the rigidity of polynomials in the complex plane by S. Smale, which was later revised and expanded, and a comprehensive analysis of the convergence theory for discrete quadratic forms by the first and fourth authors, which was originally presented at INDMAT 2019. Furthermore, this research delves into the theoretical framework of the burdens and develops a classification that includes extremal burdens, which are characterized by constant, semipositive, and positive properties. A study on the relationship between extremal burdens and their respective characteristics via a circumferential extremal burden is also a novel aspect of this work. A additional findings related to the theory of logarithmic burdens and its connections to complex variables and operator theory are also provided. A accompanying appendix is included to illustrate an example involving the concept of logarithmic burden polynomials as it relates to a weighted square with uniformly distributed weights and varying sizes. Moreover, this research delves into the theoretical framework of the burdens and their respective characteristics via a classification that includes extremal burdens and a novel aspect of this work involves a study on the relationship between extremal burdens and their respective characteristics via a circumferential extremal burden. A theory introduced in this study aims to combat the challenges of the Huber method by forgoing the requirement of positivity for the logarithmic burden. A central idea explored in this study involves a systematic approach to determining the complexity of the logarithmic burden, which is assessed through a metric that takes into account its discrete normal form. A additional findings related to the theory of logarithmic burden polynomials as it relates to a weighted square with uniformly distributed weights and varying sizes are also provided in an accompanying supplement. A related study involving the concept of logarithmic burden polynomials as it relates to a square with regularly increasing weights is presented in four separate parts, which provide an alternative method of proving the main results. The growing need to analyze and manage large amounts of text has driven the development of text summarization in various fields, including law, finance, and healthcare. However, generating high-quality summaries remains a complex task, particularly when dealing with limited human resources and tight project timelines. The rise of crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) aims to facilitate text summarization by leveraging the skills of a distributed workforce. The problem lies in efficiently identifying and assigning qualified workers to specific projects; given the platform's vast user base, it is often difficult to gauge workers' expertise prior to assignment. This research examines and addresses this challenge, focusing on locating MTurk users capable of producing high-quality summaries. The study establishes and evaluates, through extensive experimentation, a multi-faceted approach to identify and assess summarization experts. The methodology involves creating a standardized evaluation framework with both human and automated components, as well as implementing a double-pricing system to incentivize top-performing workers to participate in a talent pool. The results show that by targeting this talent pool, projects can efficiently tap into a large pool of experienced summarization experts. The study also introduces a new BERT-based model, BART-Sum, to support worker selection by blending linguistic and summarization skills. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the quality of summaries produced by this talent pool against those of novice MTurk users. The study's findings highlight the importance of talent pools in leveraging the full potential of the MTurk platform, and provides a framework for identifying and retaining top-performing experts in various fields. The study's code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/kenneyy/MTurkSummarization. The study's findings were presented at the IJCAI 2020 conference. The study's objectives were expanded to cover multiple crowdsourcing platforms in https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-56513-1_39. The study's work was recognized at the 2020 ACM SIGKDD Workshop on Machine Learning for and with Societal Information at https://sites.google.com/view/societyal, and the 2020 IEEE International Workshop on Advances in Spectral Based Spatial Time Analysis at https://sites.google.com/view/astsa2020. The study's work in talent pool construction was recognized at the 2019 CLEURWs, and the 2019 ICER. The primary author of this paper presented their work at the 2019 BlackBoxN

This study addresses this gap by introducing TS2-Net, a novel token-level transformer model that combines shift and selection operations to dramatically speed up retrieval without compromising accuracy. By integrating underlying token retrieval mechanisms, TS2-Net significantly outperformed state-of-the-art models in text-clip retrieval and achieved new benchmarks in retrieval efficiency. As a result, we generate new standards for evaluating and analyzing data from these experiments.

The concept of "locally typical" measure algebras is introduced and an explicit description of the type of such measures is provided. Additionally, through the application of "Linnik's principle" and "Weil's estimate", it can be shown that any locally typical measure algebra has a total size of $\sigma(G_{n}(k)) \ll 1$. The key benefits of advanced artificial intelligence methods, such as deep learning, have not been thoroughly analyzed when it comes to the underlying principles that enable their improvement. This lack of understanding results in the majority of enhancements being empirical and unpredictable, increasing the risk of failure. This paper adopts a novel, high-level approach that offers a theoretical framework for improving deep neural networks. This framework, called Enhance-AI, utilizes domain-agnostic concepts including problem complexity, model representativeness, and the interplay between details and overall performance. It provides measurable objectives and practical strategies for improving these key aspects. The authors have previously demonstrated the applicability of these theories in select domains. This paper presents a summary of the main outcomes and their practical implications. The goal of this research is to establish a more robust and predictable foundation for the development of next-generation artificial intelligence methods that can increase their effectiveness and robustness beyond current state-of-the-art achievements. The proposed framework is available at https://github.com/RTG-EU/Enhance-AI. An associated software package can be found at https://github.com/RTG-EU/Deep-EO. This work extends our previous research on the theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence, including references https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-21112-5 and https.//arxiv.org/2102.16548. Additional relevant research can be found at https://arxiv.org/1609.02456. The study was conducted as part of the RTG-EU project. The funding was provided by the Dutch Research Council (NWO Grant No. 31465). The work is protected by copyright and can be found under https.//enhance-ai.org/copyright. However, directly differentiating through the argmin operation that enforces sparsity is impractical due to its non-differentiable nature. Our approach uses the Kantorovich-Radon transform to convert the sparsity constraint into a set of differentiable equations. This enables us to use optimization techniques to solve the sparse optimization problem in a more efficient manner. We derive the closed-form solution of the Kantorovich-Radon transform and develop a new loss function that facilitates tensor flow implementation. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on untrained parameters, finetuning, and unsupervised feature learning. Additionally, we provide a novel sparsity-based error metric and use it to analyze the internal representations learned by our method. We demonstrate the ability of our approach to learn more sparse features compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we observed improved performance when fine-tuning pre-trained features with our sparsity method. We also achieved state-of-the-art results with our approach to unsupervised feature learning. Specifically, we outperformed existing methods by achieving improved sparsity in the IRIS dataset features and enhanced performance on the STL10 dataset with our learned features. The source code for our approach has been made publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/andreberg/spartan. While researchers have extensively studied the impact of code smells on the maintenance of software in terms of metrics and developer feedback, there is a lack of research examining the distinct perspective of developers who identify and address these issues. This study aims to fill this gap by examining the perspective of developers who identify test code smells and how they perceive these issues in relation to their overall coding experience. An online survey involving 112 developers who identified test code smells indicated that a significant majority (79%) considered these issues serious, with 68% stating they had encountered such issues before. Furthermore, developers expressed a sense of frustration and disappointment in encountering test code smells. Interestingly, despite the developers' awareness of the frequency and severity of test code smells, a considerable 57% of the developers stated they had not reported these issues, with a substantial 35% attributing their inaction to a lack of relevant information as justification. Our analysis revealed two primary motivations underlying developers' actions in responding to test code smells, namely their desire to achieve personal satisfaction or professional growth. A possible explanation for the seeming indifference of developers in addressing test code smells includes their individual motivations, limitations in reporting mechanisms and the absence of clear guidance. Researchers and practitioners are encouraged to explore methods for enhancing the information available to developers and creating a supportive environment that motivates them to actively identify, report and refine test code smells. An empirical case study involving 18 developers was conducted to investigate an intervention strategy focused on motivating developers to actively identify and refine test code smells. Results indicated a significant correlation between a developer's level of satisfaction with their current coding environment and their willingness to refine test code smells. Our findings also revealed three effective strategies in motivating developers to address test code smells: providing detailed and specific feedback, fostering a supportive environment that recognizes and rewards efforts to improve coding quality, and enabling developers to set their own goals and aspirations. Results also showed a reverse relationship between developers' confidence in their ability to refine test code smells and their actual ability to do so. Moreover, results indicated a significant relationship between a developer's satisfaction with their current coding environment and their ability to refine test code smells. Results also showed a significant relationship between a developer's preference for procedural programming and their ability to refine test code smells. Interestingly, results of the case study indicated a significant relationship between a developer's level of agreement with the importance of refining test code smells and their actual ability to refine them. Results also showed that refining test code smells within an agile framework was not a significant predictor of a developer's level of satisfaction with their current coding environment

A new method for learning a deep, dimensionally reduced representation of data is presented, based on the Wasserstein distance, to effectively tackle high-dimensional, complex learning tasks with few labeled examples. Our approach modifies the standard Wasserstein distance by introducing a least squares term, reduces sensitivity to hyperparameters, and offers a well-defined loss function for training neural networks. This new method performs at least as well as other distance-based techniques, and can be used with unlabeled data to achieve state-of-the-art results for semi-supervised classification tasks. Additionally, it demonstrates excellent performance on clustering and unsupervised learning tasks. Our implementation is available on GitHub under the term 'wadore'. Evaluation metrics and experimental settings are similar to those used in the KCN paper. Our approach outperforms various baseline methods in different scenarios. 

Video classification with few examples: The goal of this task is to classify video segments into pre-defined categories using a limited number of labeled examples. Our method, trained without segmentation, competes with state-of-the-art techniques using the KCN approach, but without its high dependence on hyperparameters and overly complex architecture. Unlabeled data is used to define a Gram matrix through unsupervised learning, and a limited number of labeled examples are used for training. Our results show that our method, trained without a convolutional network, achieves high performance and is at least as good as KCN, but with a smaller network. This capability is derived from the ability to transform the structure of the Wasserstein matrix into a kernel that can be used as a low-dimensional, linear representation of the data. 

Clustering: The input data is transformed into a low-dimensional, linear representation and clustering results are obtained. Our method, evaluated on different datasets, competes with state-of-the-art techniques and achieves the best results in terms of purity and average precision. 

Unsupervised domain adaptation: This is a task where we learn a representation of data from a known domain that is applicable to an unknown domain with no labeled data. Our method, learned with unlabeled data, is applied to the moving chair domain where there are no labels. During testing, a cycle of transformations is applied between the source and target domains, and the label-free representation is evaluated. Our method, learned with unlabeled data, is able to perform the task as well as supervised methods, and is at least as good as other distance-based techniques.
